title: MOD 03: ACLs, Syslog, NTP, CDP/LLDP & File Transfer

lessons.title: Standard ACLs
lessons.content:
1. Definitions and Terminology

  • Access Control Lists (ACLs): These are network security tools used to control who can access different parts of a network.
  • The Security Guard Analogy: ACLs work like "guards" standing between hosts and allowing or stopping data transmission based on the rules assigned to them. Just as a physical security guard checks a list, the router checks the ACL to decide if a device has permission to communicate.
  • Access Control Entries (ACEs): These are the individual, sequential rules that define the filter criteria within an Access Control List.

2. How ACLs Work & Processing Logic

  • Top-to-Bottom Logic: Access Control Entries (ACEs) in an access list are checked one at a time, starting strictly from the top and moving down.
  • First Match and Stop: When a packet matches a rule, the router applies the action (permit or deny) and stops checking further rules in the ACL. It does not matter if a later rule is more specific.
  • The "Implicit Deny" Rule:
    • If a packet does not match any rule in the ACL, it is automatically blocked and dropped.
    • This happens because every ACL has a hidden, default rule at the very end called "implicit deny" (essentially, an invisible access-list deny any).
    • Troubleshooting Note: If you configure an ACL with only deny rules, it will block all traffic. You must add a permit any command at the end of the ACL to make sure other traffic can pass.

3. Applying ACLs to Interfaces

An ACL is completely inactive on the network until it is applied to a specific router interface and direction:

  1. Inbound (IN): Controls traffic entering the interface. Inbound ACLs process packets before routing is done.
  2. Outbound (OUT): Controls traffic leaving the interface. Outbound ACLs process packets after routing is done.
  3. Interface Constraint: You can only apply one ACL per interface per direction (one for inbound and one for outbound). Applying a new ACL on the same interface/direction will replace the previous one [image on page 59].

4. Standard Numbered ACLs

  • Filtering Characteristic: Standard ACLs filter traffic based on source IP addresses only. They cannot inspect ports or destination addresses.
  • Numeric Ranges: Cisco routers use the numbers 1 to 99 and 1300 to 1999.
  • Command Syntax: 
Router(config)# access-list <1-99 | 1300-1999> {permit | deny}

```

* Host Keyword Abbreviation: Instead of typing a wildcard mask of `0.0.0.0` for a single host IP, you can use the keyword `host` before the IP.

Example:* `access-list 1 deny 1.1.1.1 0.0.0.0` is identical to `access-list 1 deny host 1.1.1.1` [image on page 15].

* Any Keyword Abbreviation: To match all traffic, use the keyword `any` instead of `0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255`.

Example:* `access-list 1 permit any`.

  • Applying to an Interface: 
Router(config-if)# ip access-group  {in | out}

```

5. Standard Named ACLs

  • Advantage: Named ACLs are easier to remember and manage because they use descriptive names (like BLOCK_ALI or TO_172.16.2.0/24) instead of numbers.
  • Command Syntax: 
Router(config)# ip access-list standard

```

(Note: You must include the word "ip" before standard named ACL commands, which is different from numbered standard ACLs [image standard named command]).

  • Sequence Numbers: Within named ACL sub-configuration, the router automatically assigns sequence numbers in steps of 10 (e.g., 10, 20, 30) so you can insert or modify rules later without deleting the entire ACL.
  • Applying to an Interface: 
Router(config-if)# ip access-group  {in | out}

6. Standard ACL Placement Rule

  • Standard ACLs should always be applied as close to the destination of the traffic as possible.
  • Why? Since standard ACLs can only filter by source IP, applying them close to the source would block the device from accessing all other networks, which is too restrictive. Placing them near the destination ensures only the target network is protected.

lessons.title: Extended ACLs
lessons.content:
1. Introduction and Differences

  • Granular Control: Unlike standard ACLs, extended ACLs give you much more detailed control over what gets through.
  • Filtering Fields: Extended ACLs can filter traffic based on:
    1. Layer 4 Protocol (e.g., TCP, UDP, ICMP, IP).
    2. Source IP Address.
    3. Destination IP Address.
    4. Port Numbers (Source and Destination).
  • Example: A standard ACL can only block all traffic to a server. An extended ACL allows you to permit web traffic (HTTP/HTTPS) while blocking ICMP (pings) to the exact same server.

2. Numeric Ranges and Command Anatomy

  • Numeric Ranges: Cisco routers use the numbers 100 to 199 and 2000 to 2699.
  • Command Syntax: 
Router(config)# access-list <100-199 | 2000-2699> {permit | deny}

[operator ]

``` [image of command anatomy on page 29]

  • Protocol Numbers: If a protocol is not explicitly listed by name, you can specify its IP protocol header number:
    • ICMP: Protocol number 1.
    • TCP: Protocol number 6.
    • UDP: Protocol number 17.
  • Operators:
    • eq (equal to)
    • neq (not equal to) [image command anatomy]
    • lt (less than) [image command anatomy]
    • gt (greater than) [image command anatomy]
  • Help Tool: You can type the ? command at any point during configuration to see a list of available protocol options and port services.

3. Common Ports and Protocols

  • HTTP: TCP Port 80
  • HTTPS: TCP Port 443
  • SMTP: TCP Port 25
  • SSH: TCP Port 22
  • Telnet: TCP Port 23
  • FTP: TCP Ports 20 (Data) and 21 (Control)
  • TFTP: UDP Port 69
  • DNS: UDP Port 53 [image protocol and ports on page 35]
  • DHCP: UDP Ports 67 (Server) and 68 (Client) [image protocol and ports on page 35]
  • NTP: UDP Port 123 [image protocol and ports on page 35]

4. Extended ACL Placement Rule

  • Extended ACLs should always be applied as close to the source of the traffic as possible.
  • Why? Placing them near the source stops unwanted traffic from traveling across the entire network, preventing unnecessary consumption of bandwidth and routing resources [image on page 35].

lessons.title: Syslog and NTP
lessons.content:
1. Internal Clock and Manual Timing

  • Internal Clock: Every Cisco device has an internal clock (hardware calendar) to track time, but it is not always accurate.
  • Asterisk (): An asterisk symbol () is displayed next to the time in the log if the device's clock is inaccurate or un-synchronized.
  • Checking Time:
    • show clock: Displays current time and timezone (defaults to UTC).
    • show clock detail: Displays time along with its precise synchronization source.
  • Manual Adjustment: Adjust the clock using the clock set command in privileged EXEC mode (not global config mode). Manual settings are not saved to the device's running configuration.
    • Syntax: Router# clock set hh:mm:ss <1-31> [image on page 48].
    • Once set manually, show clock detail will display: Time source is user configuration.

2. Network Time Protocol (NTP)

  • Purpose: NTP synchronizes clocks among time servers and client devices so that logging and debugging messages have accurate, matching time stamps.
  • Commands:
    • ntp master {stratum-level}: Sets the device as an NTP master server relying on its own internal clock. (Supports values 1 to 15 [image on page 49]).
    • ntp server {address | hostname}: Sets the device to sync with an external NTP server (acts as a client first to sync time, then can serve it to others).
  • The Stratum Hierarchy:
    • A stratum is a value from 0 to 15 indicating a device's distance from the physical authoritative time source.
    • Stratum 0: The ultimate reference clocks (e.g., GPS, Atomic Clocks, Radio Clocks).
    • Stratum 1: Directly connected to a Stratum 0 physical time source. (If R1 is configured as ntp master 1, it acts as Stratum 1).
    • Stratum 2: Synchronized with a Stratum 1 device (e.g., R2 synchronizing with R1 is Stratum 2).
    • Stratum 16: Indicates that the device is not synchronized and is no longer receiving time updates.
  • Verification:
    • show ntp status: Verifies synchronization state, stratum level, and the reference IP address.
      • NTP Master Note: On an NTP master, the reference is 127.127.1.1 (the loopback address representing its own internal clock).
    • show ntp associations: Displays detailed connection stats for all linked NTP servers and their stratum levels.

3. Syslog (System Message Logging)

  • Purpose: The standard way for network devices to record events (such as link up/down, OSPF neighbor changes, or system restarts).
  • RAM Volatility (The Danger of No Server):
    • By default, logs are stored in volatile RAM memory [image on page 59].
    • Crucial Exam Fact: Because RAM is temporary, all log messages are permanently lost when the router is turned off or rebooted, making post-restart troubleshooting impossible [image on page 59].
    • Solution: Deploy an external Syslog server to store log messages centrally and permanently [image syslog messages].
  • Syslog Severity Levels: Categorized into 8 levels, from 0 (most urgent emergency) to 7 (least urgent debug):
    • Level 0 - Emergency: System unusable.
    • Level 1 - Alert: Immediate action needed.
    • Level 2 - Critical: Critical conditions.
    • Level 3 - Error: Error conditions.
    • Level 4 - Warning: Warning conditions.
    • Level 5 - Notice: Normal but significant event (e.g. Interface link up/down).
    • Level 6 - Informational: Normal informational updates.
    • Level 7 - Debugging: Detailed output used for troubleshooting.
  • Syslog Configuration Command: To forward logs with high-precision millisecond timestamps to an external server: 
Router(config)# logging 12.0.0.2
Router(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec

``` [image on page 58]

lessons.title: CDP and LLDP
lessons.content:
1. Introduction to Layer 2 Discovery Protocols

  • Layer 2 Operation: These protocols work strictly at Layer 2 (Data Link Layer) of the OSI model and do not use IP addresses to exchange data.
  • Shared Information: Hostname, IP address, device capabilities (e.g. Router or Switch), platform model, and port ID.
  • Security Risk: Because discovery protocols transmit detailed info (like exact IOS software version and IP addresses) in clear text, a threat actor can easily sniff this data to plan an attack.
  • Best Practice: Disable both protocols globally or on all interfaces connected to untrusted networks (like edge user interfaces or ISP links).

2. Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP)

  • Cisco Proprietary: Only works between directly connected Cisco devices.
  • Enabled by Default: Turned on automatically on all Cisco devices and interfaces.
  • Timers & Addresses:
    • Sent every 60 seconds.
    • Uses multicast MAC address: 0100.0CCC.CCCC.
    • Holdtime: 180 seconds (removes neighbor if no update is received during this period).
    • Uses CDP version 2 by default.
  • Verification: show cdp neighbors displays Device ID, Local Interface, Holdtime, Capabilities, Platform, and remote Port ID.

3. Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)

  • Open Standard: IEEE 802.1AB standard that works across devices from different vendors.
  • Disabled by Default: Usually turned off on Cisco devices and must be manually enabled.
  • Timers & Addresses:
    • Sent every 30 seconds.
    • Uses multicast MAC address: 0180.C200.000E.
    • Hold Time: 120 seconds.
    • Reinitialization Delay: A 2-second delay must pass before LLDP becomes active again after restarting the protocol.

4. Configuration Commands

  • CDP Commands:
    • Disable globally: Router(config)# no cdp run
    • Enable globally: Router(config)# cdp run
    • Disable on interface: Router(config-if)# no cdp enable
  • LLDP Commands:
    • Enable globally: Router(config)# lldp run
    • Interface transmit/receive config: 
Router(config-if)# lldp transmit
Router(config-if)# lldp receive

  • Verification Commands:
    • show cdp neighbors / show lldp neighbors
    • show cdp neighbors detail (reveals neighbor IP addresses and IOS software version).

lessons.title: FTP and TFTP
lessons.content:
1. General File System and Purposes

  • Purpose: Used to upgrade Cisco IOS operating system images or backup and restore device configuration files.
  • Cisco IOS File Systems: Verified via the show file systems command.
    • flash: Storage area where the bootable Cisco IOS software image .bin file is saved.
    • nvram: Internal non-volatile memory storing the startup-config.
    • network: Represents external file destinations (like TFTP or FTP servers).
    • opaque: Storage used strictly for internal system processes.
  • Verification: show version verifies the running IOS image name. The presence of K9 in the software image name indicates the device supports cryptography and encryption (such as SSH).

2. File Transfer Protocol (FTP)

  • Layer 4 Transport: Uses reliable, connection-oriented TCP.
  • Ports: TCP Port 20 (Data transfer) and TCP Port 21 (Control connections).
  • Security: Requires mandatory authentication (username and password) to log in, making it more secure than TFTP.

3. Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP)

  • Layer 4 Transport: Uses fast but unreliable, connectionless UDP.
  • Port: UDP Port 69.
  • Security: Has zero authentication or encryption. Files travel in clear, plain text.
  • Use Case: Recommended only for transferring small files in highly secure, tightly controlled local area networks.

4. Interactive File Transfer Procedures

  • To download an image from a TFTP server to flash: 
Router# copy tftp: flash:

Address or name of remote host []? 172.16.1.100

Source filename []? c2600-i-mz.122-28.bin

Destination filename [c2600-i-mz.122-28.bin]? [Press Enter]

```

(Note: Progress is marked by exclamation points `!`. Successful transfer ends with `[OK - ... bytes]`).

  • To backup flash configurations to an FTP server: First, configure the FTP credentials on the router: 
Router(config)# ip ftp username cisco
Router(config)# ip ftp password cisco

Then run the copy command:

Router# copy flash: ftp:

Source filename []? isr4300-universalk9.16.06.04.SPA.bin

Address or name of remote host []? 172.16.1.100

Destination filename [isr4300-universalk9.16.06.04.SPA.bin]? WEschools

```

1. Key Points to Remember

  1. Top-Down Processing: ACL rules are evaluated sequentially from top to bottom. Once a match is found, processing stops.
  2. Volatile Logs: Local system logs are saved in volatile RAM and are completely lost when the router reboots or is powered off [image on page 59]. Set up an external Syslog server to prevent this [image syslog messages].
  3. Stratum 0 vs. Stratum 16: Stratum 0 devices are physical hardware reference clocks (GPS, atomic clocks). Stratum 16 indicates a completely un-synchronized state.
  4. K9 IOS Flag: Seeing K9 in a Cisco IOS filename indicates cryptographic and secure connection support (e.g. SSH).

2. Important Exam Points

  1. ACL Ranges:
    • Standard ACLs range from 1-99 and 1300-1999.
    • Extended ACLs range from 100-199 and 2000-2699.
    • Fictional Ranges Trap: An access-list statement using a number outside these ranges (like access-list 250 ... for a standard ACL) is syntax-incorrect.
  2. CDP/LLDP Timers:
    • CDP sends updates every 60s (Holdtime 180s).
    • LLDP sends updates every 30s (Holdtime 120s).
  3. Optimal Placement:
    • Standard ACL: Close to destination.
    • Extended ACL: Close to source.
  4. Wildcard Calculation Example: A subnet range of 10.120.160.0 with wildcard mask 0.0.7.255 covers all IP addresses from 10.120.160.0 to 10.120.167.255.

3. Commonly Tested Topics from the Question Bank

  1. Implicit Deny Behavior: If a packet fails to match any rule, it gets dropped due to the implicit deny rule.
  2. Inbound vs. Outbound Filtering: Inbound ACLs process packets before routing; outbound ACLs process packets after routing is complete.
  3. Named ACL Command Syntax: Always write "ip" before named ACL configuration entries (e.g., ip access-list standard ...).
  4. NTP Associations Check: Entering show ntp status on a configured NTP master displays reference clock 127.127.1.1.

description: 5 lessons covering ACLs, Syslog, NTP, CDP/LLDP & File Transfer.

title: MOD 04: Routing Protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP, FHRP)

lessons.title: Dynamic Routing Protocols- Multi Area OSPF
lessons.content:
### 1. Introduction and Routing Basics

In previous units (such as Unit 9), routing was managed using static routes, default static routes, and floating static routes. While effective for small setups, larger networks require automated management.

Dynamic Routing Protocols are special protocols that help routers in a network automatically find the best path to send data.

  • Key Advantage: Paths do not need to be configured by hand every time network changes occur. This makes networks significantly faster to adapt and much easier to manage.
  • How Routers Learn Routes: Routers learn and add routes to their routing tables in exactly three ways:
    1. Connected Routes: Learned directly from active physical network connections.
    2. Static Routes: Manually set by a network administrator.
    3. Dynamic Routing Protocols: Learned automatically through pathfinding routing protocols.

### 2. How Routing Works in a Network

#### A. Convergence

Convergence is the process where all routers in a network share routing information and work together to maintain consistent, updated, and agreed-upon routing tables, ensuring that data reaches its destination even when network changes occur.

#### B. Metrics and Route Selection

  • Metric: A value used by dynamic routing protocols to measure and decide the best path to a target subnet. A lower metric indicates a better, faster, or more efficient route.
  • Route Selection Example from the Unit: Imagine Router R1, Router R2, and Router R3.
    • R2 is connected to subnet 172.16.10.0/23.
    • R2 shares its path to this subnet directly with both R1 and R3.
    • R3 learns the path from R2, then advertises it to R1 as well.
    • R1 now has two options to reach subnet 172.16.10.0/23:
      1. A direct path from R2 with a metric of 1.
      2. An indirect path via R3 with a metric of 2.
    • Outcome: Since a lower metric is better, R1 selects the path through R2 and adds it to its routing table.

### 3. Interior and Exterior Routing Protocols

IP routing protocols are divided into two main categories based on operational scope:

  1. Interior Gateway Protocols (IGP): Used to route data within a single network or Autonomous System (AS).
  2. Exterior Gateway Protocols (EGP): Used to connect and route data between different networks or Autonomous Systems.

#### What is an Autonomous System (AS)?

An Autonomous System (AS) is a group of routers controlled by a single organization (such as a school, university, or company) that operates under common routing rules.

  • Autonomous System Number (ASN): Each AS is uniquely identified on the global Internet by a special number called an ASN.
  • Control Body: ASNs are controlled, allocated, and assigned globally by IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) to ensure uniqueness.
  • Example: A school's network acts as an AS. Within the school, an IGP manages internal routing, but if the school connects to an external network like the Internet, an EGP is required. BGP is the only EGP in active use today.

### 4. Comparing IGPs

Organizations can choose from several internal gateway protocols based on their design needs. The most common are:

  • OSPF (Open Shortest Path First): A link-state routing protocol.
  • EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol): An advanced distance-vector (or hybrid) protocol.

#### Algorithms

A routing protocol uses an algorithm, which is a predefined set of rules that helps it learn, calculate, and choose the best path for data to travel.

  • OSPF uses the Dijkstra (Shortest Path First) algorithm.
  • EIGRP uses the Diffusing Update Algorithm (DUAL).

### 5. Classful vs. Classless Routing Protocols

Understanding the difference between classful and classless behaviors is crucial for network design and exam questions:

FeatureClassful Routing ProtocolsClassless Routing Protocols
Subnet Mask InformationDo NOT send subnet masks in routing updates.Send subnet masks along with IP addresses.
Subnet Size ConstraintsAssume all subnets in the network are the same size.Allow for different subnet sizes in the network.
VLSM SupportNo support for Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM).Full support for VLSM, allowing optimized address allocation.
Mask DeterminationAssume default masks based on standard IP address classes (A, B, or C).Mask is explicitly defined per route (e.g., /24, /25).
ExamplesRIPv1OSPF, EIGRP, RIPv2
FlexibilityVery rigid and less flexible.Highly flexible and efficient network design.

  • Classful Example: If classful RIPv1 advertises Class C network 192.168.1.0, it assumes the default mask 255.255.255.0 for all subnets.
  • Classless Example: A classless protocol can advertise 192.168.1.0/24 (mask 255.255.255.0) and 192.168.1.128/25 (mask 255.255.255.128) in the same network.

### 6. Choosing the Best Route

When a router has multiple candidate paths to a destination, it uses two sequential criteria to select the absolute best path:

#### Step 1: Longest Match

The router will choose the path that matches the most consecutive bits of the destination IP address (the longest subnet mask).

  • Example: If a packet's destination IP is 192.168.1.10, and the router has two matching routes:
    1. 192.168.1.0/24 (checks the first 24 bits)
    2. 192.168.0.0/16 (checks the first 16 bits)
  • Decision: The router will select 192.168.1.0/24 because it matches more bits of the target address, making it a more specific match.

#### Step 2: Administrative Distance (AD)

If two routes are learned from different protocols but match equally (i.e. they are for the exact same destination subnet prefix and length), the router breaks the tie using Administrative Distance (AD).

  • Definition: AD is a numerical value that represents the trustworthiness of a routing source.
  • Rule: The lower the Administrative Distance, the more trusted the routing source is.
  • Standard AD Values:
    • Directly Connected: 0
    • Static Route: 1
    • EIGRP: 90
    • OSPF: 110
    • RIP: 120
  • Example: If a router learns the exact same network via an EIGRP route (AD 90) and an OSPF route (AD 110), it will prefer the EIGRP route because of its lower administrative distance.

lessons.title: OSPF Routing Protocol
lessons.content:
### 1. Introduction to Link-State Protocols

Link-state protocols like OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) do not simply look at distance; they work by allowing all routers to build a complete, identical map of the network topology.

#### Link-State Advertisements (LSAs)

OSPF routers share and synchronize topology information using messages called Link-State Advertisements (LSAs).

  • LSA Contents:
    • The sending router's unique Router ID (RID).
    • Directly connected networks/subnets.
    • Directly connected neighboring OSPF routers.
    • Link Costs (used to measure the performance and bandwidth efficiency of the path).
    • The overall structure of the network.
  • LSA Security Note: LSAs do NOT contain security passwords or sensitive router keys.

### 2. OSPF Operation (The Three Phases)

OSPF establishes and maintains routing in three main stages:

  1. Becoming Neighbors (Stage One): Physically connected routers send "Hello" messages to discover each other and check compatibility.
  2. Exchanging Databases (Stage Two): Routers synchronize their databases by exchanging all network LSAs.
  3. Adding the Best Routes (Stage Three): Each router runs the SPF (Dijkstra) algorithm on its synchronized database to calculate the shortest path to each subnet and copies these optimal paths into its routing table.

### 3. OSPF Neighbor Conditions (Strict Adjacency Rules)

For two OSPF routers to become neighbors and exchange LSAs, they must satisfy five strict conditions:

  1. Same Subnet / Network: Both physical interfaces must be configured with IP addresses belonging to the same network segment.
  2. Hello and Dead Timers:
    • Hello Timers: Keep-alive check-in messages sent regularly to confirm the other router is still online (e.g. every 10 seconds by default).
    • Dead Timers: The maximum time a router will wait for a Hello packet before declaring its neighbor "dead" or offline (e.g. 40 seconds / 4x Hello by default).
    • Adjacency Requirement: The Hello and Dead timer values must match exactly on both routers. If a Hello is not received within the Dead timer window, the neighbor is cleared and routes are recalculated.
  3. Same Area ID: Both routers must have their adjacent interfaces placed in the same OSPF Area.
    • Exam Note: If Router A has its link in Area 0 and Router B has its connecting link in Area 1, they will not form a neighbor relationship.
  4. Matching Passwords (if enabled): If OSPF authentication is configured, both routers must use the exact same password (secret handshake) to trust each other.
  5. Unique Router ID (RID): To avoid topology confusion, every router in the OSPF domain must have an absolutely unique identifier. If two routers have duplicate RIDs, they will fail to form a stable adjacency.

### 4. OSPF Backbone Area (Area 0)

OSPF uses a hierarchical design to control routing updates.

  • Area 0 is known as the Backbone Area.
  • Backbone Requirement: All other configured areas must connect directly to Area 0.
  • Role: It acts as the main transit road, moving routing information quickly and efficiently between different areas. A stable, properly configured Area 0 is vital for overall network health.

### 5. Router ID (RID) Selection Hierarchy

To participate in OSPF, every router must determine its unique 32-bit Router ID. The router selects its RID using the following strict hierarchy:

┌──────────────────────────────┐

│ Is RID configured manually? │

└──────────────┬───────────────┘

│ Yes

▼

┌──────────────────────────┐

│ Use manual router-id IP │

└──────────────────────────┘

│ No

▼

┌──────────────────────────────────┐

│ Is a Loopback interface active? │

└──────────────┬───────────────────┘

│ Yes

▼

┌──────────────────────────────┐

│ Use highest active Loopback │

│ IP address │

└──────────────────────────────┘

│ No

▼

┌──────────────────────────────────┐

│ Use highest active physical IP │

│ address │

└──────────────────────────────────┘

  • OSPF Process ID: A locally significant number used to identify the specific OSPF process instance running on the router. It is a value between 1 and 65,535.
  • Exam Trap: The OSPF Process ID does NOT need to match between neighboring routers to establish a neighbor adjacency. However, keeping them consistent is recommended for administrative simplicity.

### 6. OSPF Wildcard Masks

In OSPF network commands, the wildcard mask determines which local interfaces will participate in the routing process by comparing the interface's IP against the network statement:

  • Binary Rule:
    • 0 means the router must check and match that octet.
    • 255 means the router can ignore that octet.

#### Wildcard Mask Meanings:

  • 0.0.0.0: All four octets must match exactly (points to a single host IP).
  • 0.0.0.255: The first three octets must match, but the last octet can be anything.
  • 0.0.255.255: Only the first two octets must match exactly, ignoring the last two.
  • 0.255.255.255: Only the first octet must match, ignoring the last three.
  • 255.255.255.255: All IP addresses match (wildcard ignore-all).

#### Command Configuration Examples:

  • network 10.1.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0: Matches any interface starting with IP 10.1.X.X.
  • network 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 area 0: Matches any interface starting with IP 10.X.X.X.
  • network 10.1.13.1 0.0.0.0 area 0: Matches one exact host interface IP 10.1.13.1.
  • network 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 area 0: Matches all interfaces on the router.

### 7. OSPF Configuration Step-by-Step

We configure three routers (R1, R2, R3) connected in a triangle topology:

  • R1 subnets: 10.0.0.0/30 and 12.0.0.0/30
  • R2 subnets: 11.0.0.0/30 and 12.0.0.0/30
  • R3 subnets: 10.0.0.0/30 and 11.0.0.0/30

#### Step A: Configure a Loopback Interface (Preempts physical IP selection for RID)

R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface loopback 0
R1(config-if)# ip address 1.1.1.1 255.255.255.255
R1(config-if)# exit

#### Step B: Enable OSPF & Manually Hardcode Router ID

R1(config)# router ospf 10
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1

#### Step C: Configure Networks in Area 0

(Note: Always use network addresses, not interface IPs in the network statement).

R1(config-router)# network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
R1(config-router)# network 12.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
R1(config-router)# end

On R2:

R2(config)# router ospf 10
R2(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
R2(config-router)# network 11.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
R2(config-router)# network 12.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0

Note: As soon as 12.0.0.0/30 is entered, R1 and R2 form an adjacency because they share the same subnet and reside in the same area.

On R3:

R3(config)# router ospf 10
R3(config-router)# router-id 3.3.3.3
R3(config-router)# network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
R3(config-router)# network 11.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0

### 8. Verification & Troubleshooting Commands

  • show ip route: Shows the IP routing table.
    • OSPF routes are marked with the letter O.
    • Understanding Route Notation: 11.0.0.0 [110/2] via 10.0.0.2, GigabitEthernet1/0.
      • O: Route learned via OSPF.
      • 110: Administrative Distance (AD) of OSPF.
      • 2: Metric (link cost) of the route.
      • via 10.0.0.2: Next-hop IP address.
  • show ip ospf neighbor: Shows discovered neighbors and established relationships.
    • Displays: Neighbor ID (Router ID), Pri (Interface priority), State (Should ideally be FULL/DR or FULL/BDR), Dead Time (recounting timers), Address (interface IP of neighbor), and Interface (local exit interface).

lessons.title: EIGRP Routing Protocol
lessons.content:
### 1. Introduction to EIGRP

  • Type: EIGRP is an advanced distance-vector (often called hybrid) protocol.
  • Standardization: Created by Cisco and remains exclusive to Cisco devices.
  • Function: Tells routers how far away other networks are and the exact cost of reaching them.
  • VLSM Support: Unlike classful RIPv1, EIGRP includes subnet mask information in routing updates, allowing classless network design.

### 2. EIGRP Neighbor Adjacency Requirements

For two EIGRP routers to become neighbors, five compatibility conditions must match on both routers:

  1. Same Subnet / Network: Interfaces must be on the same subnet.
  2. Hello / ACK Exchange: Routers must actively exchange EIGRP Hello and Acknowledgment packets.
  3. Matching AS Numbers: Both routers must be configured with the exact same Autonomous System (AS) Number.
  4. Matching Metrics (K-Values): The metric weight settings (K-values) must be identical.
  5. Unique Router ID (RID): Each router must have a unique Router ID.
    • Timer Exception: Unlike OSPF, EIGRP Hello and Hold timers do NOT need to match on neighboring routers to form a successful relationship.

#### Hello and Hold Timers

  • Hello Intervals: Hello packets are sent every 5 seconds on high-speed links and every 60 seconds on slower links.
  • Hold Timer: Specifies how long a router waits for a Hello packet before declaring its neighbor "dead".
    • Default Hold Time: 3 times the hello interval (usually 15 seconds on fast links and 180 seconds on slower links).
    • Important Operational Note: If you manually adjust the Hello timer, the Hold timer does not automatically change; you must adjust it separately.

### 3. Exchanging Data and Path Selection

  • OSPF vs. EIGRP Topology View:
    • In OSPF, every router sees a full, synchronized map of the entire network topology.
    • In EIGRP, a router only knows its immediate neighbors and their reported path details ("routing by rumor").
  • Reliable Transport Protocol (RTP): EIGRP uses its own transport protocol (RTP) instead of UDP/TCP to manage routing communication. RTP ensures EIGRP messages are delivered reliably and processed in the correct order using sequence numbers.
  • Diffusing Update Algorithm (DUAL): EIGRP uses the DUAL algorithm to calculate and select the best loop-free routes in the network.

### 4. Reported Distance (RD) vs. Feasible Distance (FD)

To choose the best path, EIGRP uses two key distance measurements:

  1. Reported Distance (RD) (also called Advertised Distance): The total metric for a route as advertised by a neighboring router (how far the neighbor is from the destination).
  2. Feasible Distance (FD): The total metric from the local router to the destination subnet. This is calculated by adding the local link cost to the neighbor's Reported Distance.

#### The Ahmed & Mohamed Analogy:

Imagine you are looking for Mohamed's home.

  • You ask your friend Ahmed: "Ahmed, where is Mohamed's home?"
  • Ahmed replies: "Mohamed lives exactly 2 homes away from me." This is the Reported Distance (RD = 2).
  • You calculate: "Since Ahmed is 1 home away from me, and Mohamed is 2 homes away from Ahmed, then Mohamed is exactly 3 homes away from me." This is the Feasible Distance (FD = 3).

### 5. EIGRP Route States & Tables

EIGRP routers maintain three essential tables:

  1. Neighbor Table: Tracks active physical neighbors and their timers (show ip eigrp neighbor).
  2. Topology Table: Stores all potential paths learned from neighbors (show ip eigrp topology).
  3. Routing Table: Stores only the best path for forwarding data (show ip route).

#### Active Route Roles in EIGRP:

  • Successor: The absolute best route selected by DUAL to reach a network. It has the lowest Feasible Distance (FD) and is added to the routing table to forward active data.
  • Feasible Successor (FS): A backup route that satisfies the Feasibility Condition (its RD is less than the current Successor's FD). It remains in the topology table, ready to take over instantly if the active Successor fails.

### 6. EIGRP Classical Metric Calculation

EIGRP uses five different factors, weighted by K_1 through K_5, to calculate path metrics. By default, metric calculations use Bandwidth (BW) and Delay.

  • Min. Bandwidth: Represents the slowest link speed in the entire path, scaled to a 10 Gbps reference link (10^7 divided by slowest bandwidth in kbps).
  • Total Delay: The sum of all interface delays in the path, measured in tens of microseconds (µs (microseconds)).
  • Classic Formula Factor: EIGRP multiplies the legacy 24-bit IGRP metric by 256 to create a high-precision 32-bit metric.

#### Default K-Values:

  • K_1 (Bandwidth) = 1
  • K_3 (Delay) = 1
  • K_2, K_4, K_5 (Load, Reliability) = 0

#### Streamlined Default Metric Formula:

ext{Metric} = 256 imes \left( rac{10^7}{ ext{Slowest Bandwidth (kbps)}} + rac{ ext{Sum of Delays}}{10} ight)

### 7. EIGRP Configuration step-by-step

We configure WE1, WE2, and WE3 with EIGRP in Autonomous System (AS) 20:

  • Important Operational Difference: In EIGRP, the command is router eigrp [AS-number], and the AS number must match exactly on all routers. In OSPF, the process ID does not need to match. 
WE1# configure terminal
WE1(config)# router eigrp 20
WE1(config-router)# eigrp router-id 1.1.1.1
WE1(config-router)# network 172.16.10.0 0.0.0.3
WE1(config-router)# network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3

#### EIGRP Automatic Summarization

By default, EIGRP automatically groups or summarizes subnets at classful boundaries (e.g. summarizing internal subnets into classful class A 10.0.0.0/8 or class B 172.16.0.0/16 networks) and routes them to a Null0 virtual interface.

  • Null0 Purpose: If incoming traffic does not match a more specific, detailed subnet, it gets discarded at Null0, successfully preventing routing loops.

Disabling Auto-Summary: Summarization can sometimes hide specific route details, leading to routing issues. To disable it:\

WE1(config-router)# no auto-summarization
  • (Once entered, the router will resync with neighbors to propagate specific subnet routes).

### 8. Verification & Troubleshooting Commands

  • show ip route: Displays learned routes. EIGRP routes are marked with the code D.
  • show ip eigrp topology: Displays successor and backup paths.
    • Route Codes:
      1. P (Passive): Indicates the route is stable, healthy, and ready for use. This is the ideal state.
      2. A (Active): Indicates the route is down and the router is actively querying its neighbors to search for a backup path.
  • show ip eigrp neighbor: Displays the active EIGRP neighbor table.
    • Columns and Meanings:
      1. H: The order in which the neighbor adjacency was discovered (starts at 0).
      2. Address: The physical IP address of the neighbor router.
      3. Interface: The local egress interface connected to the neighbor.
      4. Hold (sec): The countdown time remaining before the neighbor is declared dead.
      5. Uptime: Exactly how long the neighbor relationship has been established.
      6. SRTT (Smooth Round-Trip Timer): The average time in milliseconds for a packet to complete a round-trip to the neighbor and back.
      7. RTO (Retransmission Time Out): The time EIGRP waits before retransmitting a multicast packet, calculated using SRTT.
      8. Q Cnt (Queue Count): The number of EIGRP packets waiting in queue to be sent. This should always be 0. A consistently high value indicates local link congestion or packet loss.
      9. Seq (Sequence Number): The sequence number of the last update packet from that neighbor, used to track packet order and prevent duplication.

lessons.title: BGP Routing Protocol
lessons.content:
### 1. Understanding BGP & Autonomous Systems

While Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) handle routing within a single network, routing across the global Internet is managed by BGP (Border Gateway Protocol).

  • Scope: BGP connects different Autonomous Systems (AS).
  • Internal vs. External Protocol Selection: Within an Autonomous System, the organization is free to run internal protocols like OSPF, EIGRP, or RIP. However, to route data outside the AS and across the Internet, BGP is mandatory.

### 2. Autonomous System Numbers (ASN)

Every AS must have a unique identifier called an Autonomous System Number (ASN).

#### ASN Expansion (2-byte vs. 4-byte)

  • 2-Byte ASNs (16-bit): Originally, ASNs were only 2 bytes, which allowed a maximum of 65,535 unique ASNs.
  • 4-Byte ASNs (32-bit): Due to rapid internet growth and ASN exhaustion, RFC 4893 expanded the ASN field to 4 bytes. This allows for 4,294,967,295 unique ASNs.

#### Private ASNs

Certain blocks of ASNs are reserved strictly for private internal testing and use within an organization; they must never be advertised publicly on the Internet.

  • 16-Bit Private ASN Range: 64,512 through 65,535.
  • 32-Bit Private ASN Range: 4,200,000,000 through 4,294,967,294.
  • Strict Policy Warning: It is imperative to use only the ASN assigned by IANA, your service provider, or a private ASN. Using another organization's ASN without permission can cause severe internet instability, routing loops, and critical traffic loss.

### 3. BGP Peer Sessions & Routing

There are exactly two types of BGP peer sessions:

  1. iBGP (Internal BGP): Used to connect and share routes between routers inside the same Autonomous System.
  2. eBGP (External BGP): Used to connect and route data between routers in different Autonomous Systems.

#### BGP Characteristics:

  • Unicast Communication: BGP only connects directly with pre-configured peer routers and sends only unicast messages (no multicasts or broadcasts).
  • Transport Protocol: BGP uses TCP on port 179 to establish and maintain stable, reliable peer connections.
  • Path-Vector Metric: BGP is a path-vector protocol that routes data based on the AS_PATH attribute.
    • AS_PATH: A list of ASNs traversed to reach a target destination.
    • Route Selection: BGP always selects the route with the shortest AS_PATH (the route that passes through the fewest Autonomous Systems).
    • Scale: The global internet routing table contains approximately 900,000 active routes.

lessons.title: FHRP and HSRP
lessons.content:
### 1. The Need for Redundancy

Physical infrastructure components like routers, switches, power systems, and WAN cables can and do fail.

  • Single Point of Failure (SPOF): Any single hardware component, device, or link whose failure would cause a major network outage for a large portion of users.
  • High Availability: High availability is achieved by adding redundant backup devices and backup transmission links, securing a continuous path for data to travel.

### 2. First Hop Redundancy Protocols (FHRP)

A First Hop Redundancy Protocol (FHRP) allows multiple physical routers to work together and act as a single "virtual default gateway" for host devices on a local subnet.

  • "First Hop": Refers to the very first default gateway router that packets pass through on their way to external networks.
  • Virtual Router: FHRP creates a logical "virtual router" that has its own shared Virtual IP address and Virtual MAC address.
  • Device Settings: Host devices on the LAN configure their default gateway pointing to the Virtual IP address. They do not know (or need to care) which physical router is actively handling their data.

### 3. Comparing the Three Main FHRPs

ProtocolDeveloper TypeOperational CharacteristicsLoad Balancing
HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol)Cisco ProprietaryActive/Standby failover: one physical router is active, others standby.No active load balancing within a single group.
VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol)Open StandardActive/Backup failover: operates similarly to HSRP but works on any vendor.No active load balancing within a single group.
GLBP (Gateway Load Balancing Protocol)Cisco ProprietaryActive load balancing and redundancy; supports up to four routers in a group.Full active load balancing, distributing traffic evenly.

### 4. Hot Standby Router Protocol (HSRP) Mechanics

In HSRP, routers are elected to specific operational roles:

  • Active Router: Actively forwards all data traffic sent to the virtual gateway IP/MAC.
  • Standby Router: Monitors the active router using HSRP hello packets, ready to take over immediately if the active router fails.

#### The Failover Process:

  1. Under normal operation, the Active Router handles all traffic. Both routers send each other HSRP Hello messages to check status.
  2. If the Active Router goes down (e.g. loses power or link), the Standby Router stops receiving Hello packets.
  3. Once the standby hold timer expires, the Standby Router instantly takes over the Virtual IP and Virtual MAC.
  4. The new active router sends a special network frame (gratuitous ARP) containing the Virtual MAC to LAN switches.
  5. Switches immediately update their MAC address tables to point to the new physical port.
  6. No client reconfiguration is needed: The hosts continue sending packets to the same Virtual IP, resulting in seamless, zero-touch failover.

### 5. HSRP Configuration Step-by-Step

We configure HSRP between R1 and R2 in group 1:

  • R1 IP: 10.1.1.1/24
  • R2 IP: 10.1.1.2/24
  • Virtual IP Address: 10.1.1.10/24

#### HSRP Priority & Election:

  • Default Priority: All HSRP routers have a default priority of 100.
  • Election Rule: The router with the highest priority wins the election to become the Active Router.
  • Boot Timing Exception: HSRP priority is only evaluated if both routers boot simultaneously. If one router boots first, it immediately becomes Active, regardless of its priority.
  • Preemption: By default, preemption is disabled. If a router with a higher priority comes online after another router has already established itself as Active, it will not reclaim the Active state unless preemption is manually enabled.

#### R1 Configuration (Primary Active - Priority 110):

R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# standby 1 ip 10.1.1.10
R1(config-if)# standby 1 priority 110

#### R2 Configuration (Backup Standby - Default Priority 100):

R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# standby 1 ip 10.1.1.10

(Naming the standby group is optional and used for administrative reference only).

### 6. Verification and continuous ping troubleshooting

To verify HSRP operations, use the following commands:

  • show standby: Displays HSRP details.
    • State: Displays whether the local router is Active or Standby.
    • Virtual IP Address: Displays the shared IP (e.g. 10.1.1.10).
    • Virtual MAC Address: Displays the active virtual MAC (e.g. 0000.0C07.AC01 for HSRP version 1).
    • Hello/Hold Timers: Default Hello is 3 seconds, default Hold is 10 seconds.
    • Active Router IP: Displays the physical IP of the current Active router.
    • Standby Router IP: Displays the physical IP of the current Standby router.
    • Priority: Displays configured vs. default priority.
    • Preemption Status: Displays Preemption disabled or enabled.

#### Continuous Ping Failover Test:

During a continuous ping test from a local host (ping -t 192.168.1.100), if you shut down the active router (R1), the ping will experience only a few seconds of packet loss before recovering as the standby router (R2) seamlessly transitions to the active role.

## Key Points to Remember

  1. Route Types: Routing tables contain three route categories: directly connected links (AD 0), manual static entries (AD 1), and dynamic protocol entries.
  2. Convergence Goal: A network is considered converged when all routers contain identical, loop-free routing paths.
  3. Classless vs. Classful: RIPv1 is a legacy classful protocol that ignores subnet masks; OSPF and EIGRP are modern classless protocols that support VLSM and different subnet sizes.
  4. Path Metrics: Dynamic routing uses metrics (hop count, link cost, or composite delay/bandwidth) to measure paths. A lower metric is always preferred.
  5. Tie-Breakers: Routers select the best route using the Longest Match first. If two matching routes have the same length prefix, the router selects the one with the lowest Administrative Distance.
  6. OSPF Hello/Dead Timers: Hellos are sent every 10 seconds, and the dead interval is 40 seconds by default. These timers must match exactly for routers to form an adjacency.
  7. Router ID (RID): OSPF and EIGRP routers require a unique RID. It is selected in order of: Manual ID -> Loopback IP -> Physical interface IP.
  8. EIGRP Metrics: EIGRP calculations use Bandwidth and Delay by default (K_1=1, K_3=1). The EIGRP metric is the 24-bit IGRP value multiplied by 256 to create a 32-bit value.
  9. Successor & FS: In EIGRP, a Successor is the active best path, and a Feasible Successor is the pre-calculated backup path.
  10. BGP Scope: BGP is a Path-Vector protocol running on TCP port 179 that connects different Autonomous Systems across the Internet.
  11. AS_PATH length: BGP selects routes with the shortest AS_PATH.
  12. ASN Ranges: ASNs expanded from 2 bytes to 4 bytes. Private ASNs exist in 16-bit (64512-65535) and 32-bit (4200000000-4294967294) ranges.
  13. FHRP Redundancy: FHRPs provide high-availability gateway redundancy by presenting multiple physical routers as a single virtual router IP/MAC.
  14. FHRP Comparison: VRRP is an open standard; HSRP and GLBP are Cisco proprietary. GLBP is unique because it supports active load balancing.
  15. HSRP Priority: Default priority is 100, and the highest priority wins the election. Preemption is disabled by default, preventing a higher-priority router from reclaiming active status unless manually enabled.

## Important Exam Points

  • LSA Contents: Be prepared for questions listing LSA parameters. Key Point: LSAs contain link costs, RID, and structure, but never passwords.
  • Adjacency Mismatches: A common troubleshooting question provides CLI configurations and asks why neighbors won't form. Check for:
    1. Area ID mismatches (e.g., R1 on Area 0 and R2 on Area 10).
    2. Subnet mismatches.
    3. Timer mismatches (Hello/Dead).
    4. Password mismatches.
  • Longest Match Calculation: Given a destination address (e.g. 192.168.1.10), identify which route the router will choose. The route with the most specific subnet mask (longest prefix) always wins, regardless of a higher metric or AD.
  • EIGRP timer matching: Unlike OSPF, EIGRP does not require matching Hello and Hold timers to establish a neighbor relationship. It does, however, require matching AS numbers and K-values.
  • EIGRP topology codes: On the exam, you may be shown a show ip eigrp topology output and asked what code "P" means. It stands for Passive, meaning the route is stable, healthy, and correct.
  • BGP peer configuration error: If an administrator configures BGP using an unallocated public ASN or another company's ASN, it will cause unauthorized routing havoc, black holes, and traffic loss on the Internet.
  • HSRP boot order exception: If R1 (priority 110) boots after R2 (priority 100) has already fully booted and active election is complete, R2 remains Active because preemption is disabled by default.

## Commonly Tested Topics from the Question Bank

### 1. Match the routing protocol types with their correct descriptions:

  • Connected Route: Learned directly from a network connection.
  • Static Route: Set manually by a network administrator.
  • Dynamic Routing Protocol: Learned through automatic pathfinding protocols.
  • Classful Protocol: RIPv1.
  • Classless Protocol: OSPF, EIGRP.
  • Exterior Gateway Protocol: BGP.

### 2. Match the OSPF neighbor conditions with their descriptions:

  • Same Network: Both routers must be on the same subnet.
  • Hello and Dead Timers: Check-ins to confirm the other router is still online.
  • Same Area ID: Routers need to belong to the same OSPF area.
  • Matching Passwords: Security check; both routers must have the same password.
  • Unique Router ID: Each router must have a unique identifier to avoid confusion.

### 3. Match the EIGRP terms with their correct descriptions:

  • RD (Reported Distance): Metric of a route as advertised by a neighboring router.
  • FD (Feasible Distance): The local router's total metric to a destination network.
  • Successor: The best route to a network (installed in the routing table).
  • Feasible Successor: A pre-calculated backup route stored in the topology table.

### 4. BGP port number:

  • BGP operates over TCP port 179.

### 5. FHRP & HSRP election questions:

  • An HSRP standby router has a default priority of 100.
  • The router with the highest priority wins the election.
  • Host devices configure the shared Virtual IP address as their default gateway.
