lessons.title: Introduction to Windows Server
lessons.content:
This lesson introduces the foundation of computer networks, focusing on different architectures, server roles, operating system editions, and virtualization.

### 1. Concepts and Definitions

  • Computer Network: A group of interconnected devices that communicate and transmit data to facilitate resource sharing within an organization.
  • Operating System (OS): Acting like the "conductor of a computer orchestra," the OS coordinates and manages all software and hardware resources.
  • What is a Server?: A dedicated computer system or software application within a networked computing environment that offers specialized services, resources, or functionality to client devices (clients).
    • Analogy: Think of a server as a school library that stores a vast collection of books (data) and lends them out to students (clients) as needed.

### 2. Network Architectures: P2P vs. Client/Server

  • Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Network:
    • All computers are equal (peers) and can share files and resources directly with one another without a central server.
    • Use Cases: Most suitable for small networks or home environments.
  • Client/Server Network:
    • A centralized architecture where dedicated servers manage resources, security, data access, and application functionality.
    • Analogy: The server behaves like a teacher who holds all classroom resources (books, assignments, videos), and clients are like students requesting those resources from the teacher.
    • Use Cases: Preferred for schools and businesses due to centralized control, enhanced security, scalability, and easy resource access.

### 3. Client Operating Systems vs. Server Operating Systems

  • Client OS (e.g., Windows 10/11): Optimized primarily for personal productivity, daily computing tasks, and individual user experiences.
  • Server OS (e.g., Windows Server 2019): Specialized toolkits designed to handle complex network traffic, manage large-scale networks, secure enterprise resources, and serve the concurrent needs of multiple users simultaneously.

### 4. Hardware Server Forms

  • Blade Server: A thin, modular server designed to save physical space by fitting into a chassis that shares power, cooling, and network infrastructure with other blade units.
  • Modular Server: A flexible server architecture that allows components to be easily added, upgraded, or replaced.

### 5. Windows Server Roles and Functions

  • File Server: Responsible for file storage, sharing, and centralized file access permissions.
  • Database Server: Stores large amounts of structured data and handles queries from clients.
  • Mail Server: Stores and manages email communication and routing across the network.
  • Web Server: Hosts websites, web services, and web applications.
  • Application Server: Manages centralized applications and their execution/functionality.
  • Domain Controller (DC): Running the Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) role, it acts as a central gatekeeper to authenticate users and manage network resources.

### 6. Windows Server 2019 Features

  • Hyper-V Virtualization: Enables a single physical server to run multiple Virtual Machines (VMs) simultaneously within isolated, logical environments to optimize hardware utilization.
  • Windows Admin Center (WAC): Introduced in Windows Server 2019 as a modern, web-based management tool for local and remote server administration.
  • Installation Options:
    • Server Core: Includes only the essential components required for basic server operations. It lacks a Graphical User Interface (GUI), leading to lower overhead, higher performance, a smaller security attack surface, and remote-management design.
    • Nano Server: An ultra-lightweight installation option even smaller than Server Core, specifically optimized for cloud services, microservices, and containerized environments.
    • Desktop Experience: The traditional, full-GUI installation option.

lessons.title: Create domain and domain Controller
lessons.content:
This lesson covers the logical concepts of domains, the core role of Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS), and the essential steps of promoting a server to a Domain Controller.

### 1. Key Concepts

  • Domain: A secure, logical, and administrative boundary within a network for organizing users, groups, computers, and security policies.
    • Analogy: A domain is like a secure club where only authorized members are granted access to the club's private resources.
  • Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS): A directory service that acts as a central repository (directory) storing structured information about all users, groups, computers, and network resources. It serves as the primary system for central resource management and authorization.
  • Domain Controller (DC): A Windows Server that has been promoted with the AD DS role installed, making it the central security and administrative authority of the domain.

### 2. Core Functions of a Domain Controller

  • User Authentication: Act as "gatekeepers" to verify user credentials (usernames and passwords) when logging into the network, allowing only authorized access.
  • Access Control: Evaluates permissions to decide what resources authenticated users are allowed to access based on security groups and corporate policies.
  • Replication: Automatically synchronizes directory database changes among multiple domain controllers. This ensures data consistency across the network, provides redundancy, and delivers fault tolerance to eliminate any single point of failure.

### 3. Step-by-Step Domain Creation Procedure

  1. Configure Pre-requisites: Assign a descriptive host name (e.g., "PDC") and configure a static IP address.
  2. Choose a Unique Domain Name: This is the critical first logical setup step. Use proper domain naming practices (incorporating a valid Top-Level Domain extension like .com or .org).
  3. Install the AD DS Role: This converts the standalone server into a candidate for promotion.
  4. Promote the Server to a Domain Controller: Run the Active Directory promotion wizard to configure the new forest, root domain, and database paths.
  5. Configure DNS: Ensure DNS is properly configured with secure records and monitoring to protect network mapping.

### 4. Group Policy Management

  • Group Policy: Allows administrators to centrally manage, enforce, and restrict security policies, software installations, and system configurations across all domain-joined computers.
  • Easily Missed Exam Detail: The Group Policy Management feature can be used independently of the AD DS role itself.

lessons.title: Active directory
lessons.content:
This lesson delves deeper into the physical and logical structure of Active Directory, its database and folder layouts, promotion requirements, and automated deployment scripting.

### 1. Active Directory Logical Hierarchy

  • Forest: The absolute largest container and administrative boundary in Active Directory, comprising one or more domains. All domains within a single forest automatically establish two-way trust relationships.
    • Root Domain: The very first domain created in a new forest.
    • Child Domain: A domain joined to an existing forest that shares a contiguous namespace with its parent domain.
  • Tree: A collection of domains that share a contiguous DNS naming structure.
  • Domain: An administrative and security boundary within the forest.
  • Organizational Unit (OU): Logical containers within a domain used to organize network objects (users, groups, computers) and simplify management. They are the smallest unit to which Group Policy Objects (GPOs) can be linked and administrative control can be delegated.

### 2. Core Components and Terminology

  • Global Catalog: A central repository that stores a partial, read-only replica of all objects across every domain in the forest. It assists users in finding and accessing resources across multiple domains and facilitates multi-domain network logons.
  • Read-Only Domain Controller (RODC): A special domain controller designed for branch offices or remote locations with low physical security. It holds a read-only copy of the Active Directory database, allowing local authentication while preventing unauthorized administrative changes.
  • Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM): A specialized, offline boot mode used by administrators to repair, restore, or rebuild the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) in the event of directory database corruption.
  • NetBIOS Name: A legacy, 15-character computer nickname used in older Windows networks. Must be unique on the local network. It is maintained in modern networks to ensure backward compatibility with older operating systems (e.g., legacy industrial computers running Windows XP).
  • Directory Information Base (DIB): The Active Directory database that stores all object data, including users, groups, computers, and security policies.

### 3. Active Directory Promotion Requirements

  • Static IP Address: A static IP is strictly required for domain controllers. Dynamic IP addresses are not permitted because other domain devices must consistently locate the domain controller.
  • Descriptive Server Naming: Assign a clear, descriptive name (e.g., "PDC" or "Primary Domain Controller") before promotion to identify the server's network role.
  • Time Synchronization: Domain controller clocks must be synchronized with an accurate, standard time source. Accurate timekeeping is critical for security protocols (like Kerberos authentication) and proper network operations.
  • User Provisioning Alert: When adding a client user to a domain for the first time, you must disable the option of "changing the password at the next login" on the client account setup [see ALERT screenshot].

### 4. Active Directory Folder Paths (Crucial for Exams)

During the AD DS Configuration Wizard, administrators specify folder locations for AD data [45, see Paths screenshot]:

  • Database Folder: Stores the active directory database (NTDS.dit). Default path: C:\Windows\NTDS.
  • Log Files Folder: Stores the transaction logs. Default path: C:\Windows\NTDS.
  • SYSVOL Folder: Stands for "System Volume." It is a vital, public shared directory that stores Group Policy templates, logon/logoff scripts, and replication scripts. Default path: C:\Windows\SYSVOL. It ensures all domain-joined computers apply identical administrative guidelines.

### 5. Automated Active Directory Deployment Script

Active Directory promotion configurations can be exported as a Windows PowerShell script to automate deployment on additional servers instead of running the graphical wizard.

The Standard Deployment Script Template:

Import-Module ADDSDeployment

Install-ADDSForest `

-CreateDnsDelegation:false `

-DatabasePath "C:\Windows\NTDS" `

-DomainMode "WinThreshold" `

-DomainName "we.com" `

-DomainNetbiosName "WE" `

-ForestMode "Win2008R2" `

-InstallDns:true `

-LogPath "C:\Windows\NTDS" `

-NoRebootOnCompletion:false `

-SysvolPath "C:\Windows\SYSVOL" `

-Force:true

lessons.title: Storage, Replication and High Availability
lessons.content:
This lesson focuses on storage architectures, file systems, disk partitioning structures, high availability dynamic volumes, storage pooling, and Network Interface Card (NIC) Teaming.

### 1. File Systems: NTFS vs. ReFS

  • NTFS (New Technology File System): The default and most versatile file system for Windows Server 2019.
    • Features: Centralized file-level and folder-level permissions, built-in file encryption (EFS), security auditing, and file compression. It has no 4GB file size limit (unlike legacy FAT32 systems).
  • ReFS (Resilient File System): Engineered specifically for high-capacity, large-scale data storage and modern cloud deployment.
    • Features: Advanced data protection, metadata integrity, and automated self-healing.
    • Exception / Special Case: ReFS cannot be used to run/boot the Windows Server operating system itself.

### 2. NTFS Permissions Hierarchy

  • Full Control: Allows users to read, write, modify, delete files/folders, and dynamically change security permissions for other users.
  • Modify: Allows reading, writing, and deleting files and folders.
  • Write: Restricted to adding new files or making changes to existing files; does not allow deleting files.
  • Note: Permissions can be assigned directly to both individual users and security groups.

### 3. Physical Disk Partitioning Structures

  • Basic Disk: The standard disk type that uses standard partitions and logical drives to organize storage.
  • Dynamic Disk: Advanced disk type that allows creating dynamic volumes that can span across multiple physical drives.

### 4. Dynamic Volumes and High Availability (Exam Priority)

  • Spanned Volume: Combines free space from multiple physical disks. It writes data by filling up one disk completely before moving to the next. It can be easily expanded but offers zero fault tolerance (if one disk fails, the entire spanned volume is lost).
  • Striped Volume: Distributes data evenly across multiple physical disks to improve read and write performance. It offers zero redundancy / zero fault tolerance.
  • Mirrored Volume: Creates and maintains two identical copies of all data on two physical disks. It is heavily utilized when data protection and redundancy are priorities.
  • RAID-5 Volume: Distributes data across three or more physical disks and incorporates parity calculations. If a single disk fails, parity data is used to recover the lost data.

### 5. Storage Pools

  • Storage Pool: A software-defined storage feature that groups multiple physical hard drives into a single logical storage space.
  • Benefits: Easy scalability (adding disks dynamically), unified storage management, and maximized utilization of scattered disk space.
  • Provisioning Methods:
    • Thin Provisioning: Allocates storage space on-demand as files are written. The pool expands dynamically, saving initial hardware costs.
    • Fixed Provisioning: Immediately reserves a set, guaranteed amount of physical storage space from the pool, ensuring guaranteed volume availability.

### 6. High Availability via NIC Teaming

  • NIC Teaming: Combines multiple physical network adapters (NICs) into a single logical interface.
    • Benefits: Increased total bandwidth, automatic network traffic load balancing, and failover redundancy (network connectivity remains online if a physical adapter fails).
    • Load Balancing: The Dynamic NIC Teaming mode is highly preferred in Windows Server 2019 because it optimizes balanced load distribution and provides reliable fault tolerance.

lessons.title: Concepts of TCP/IP -- DHCP and DNS
lessons.content:
This lesson covers core TCP/IP infrastructure services: automatic IP address assignment via DHCP and name resolution via DNS.

### 1. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)

  • Purpose: Automatically assigns, leases, and manages dynamic IP addresses and IP configurations (subnet mask, gateway, DNS servers) to client devices on the network.
  • Subnet Mask: Establishes network boundaries to ensure efficient routing and device communication.
  • DHCP Scope: A consecutive range of IP addresses (from a starting IP to an ending IP) that the DHCP server is authorized to distribute to clients.
  • Exclusions: Specific IP addresses within an active scope range that are blocked from automatic assignment. Exclusions are reserved for network devices that require static IPs, such as servers, routers, and network printers.
  • DHCP Leases: Logical address agreements specifying the duration a client device can use its assigned IP address before requesting a lease renewal.

### 2. DNS (Domain Name System)

  • Purpose: Acts as the "phonebook of the internet / intranet" by translating human-readable domain names (e.g., google.com) into numerical IP addresses that computers use to locate hosts.
  • Hosts File: A local, static text file used in early networking to store manual domain-to-IP mappings. It remains the very first place a Windows operating system checks when initiating name resolution.
  • DNS Cache: A local storage on a computer that temporarily saves recently resolved domain names and IP addresses for rapid access without querying DNS servers.
  • Forward Lookup Zone: Resolves a host name into its corresponding IP address.
  • Reverse Lookup Zone: Resolves an IP address back into its host name.

### 3. Core DNS Resource Records (Exam Essentials)

  • A Record: Maps an IPv4 host name to its numerical IP address.
  • AAAA Record: Maps an IPv6 host name to its numerical IP address.
  • CNAME (Canonical Name): Creates an alias pointing to an existing canonical host name.
  • MX (Mail Exchanger): Identifies the mail servers responsible for handling email for the domain.
  • NS (Name Server): Identifies the authoritative DNS servers for a specific DNS zone.
  • PTR (Pointer): Used within Reverse Lookup Zones to map an IP address to its host name.

### 4. DNS Resolution and Queries

  • Recursive Query: A name resolution request where the client demands a definitive answer from its DNS server (either the resolved IP or an error). If the DNS server does not have the record, it will query other DNS servers (Root, TLD, etc.) on behalf of the client.
  • Iterative Query: A request where a queried DNS server returns the best answer it currently possesses (such as a referral to a TLD server further down the hierarchy) rather than querying other servers itself.
  • DNS Resolution Hierarchy:
    1. Local DNS Cache / Hosts File: First checking locations on the local device.
    2. Local DNS Server: Queries the client's configured DNS server.
    3. Root Servers: The highest level of the global DNS authority hierarchy.
    4. Top-Level Domain (TLD) Servers: DNS servers responsible for resolving TLD extensions such as .com, .org, or .edu.

### 5. Essential Command Line Syntax

Display local DNS Cache: ipconfig /displaydns

Clear / Flush local DNS Cache: ipconfig /flushdns

## Key Points to Remember

  1. Client/Server Superiority: Client/server networks are the enterprise standard because they provide centralized administration, uniform security, and scalability that peer-to-peer architectures cannot support.
  2. Domain Controller Gatekeeping: The primary functions of a domain controller are Authentication (checking credentials), Access Control (enforcing rules), and Replication (ensuring directory consistency across the network).
  3. Promotion Prerequisite: Standalone servers must have a static IP address configured before promotion to a domain controller. Dynamic IP configurations are invalid.
  4. File System Boot Limitation: While ReFS provides advanced metadata integrity and self-healing for large storage spaces, it cannot be used to boot the Windows Server operating system.
  5. Dynamic Volume Trade-Off: Striped volumes (RAID-0) offer speed but no fault tolerance. Mirrored volumes (RAID-1) write identical data to two disks, prioritizing redundancy and data safety over write speed.
  6. Thin Provisioning Advantage: Thin provisioning optimizes physical drive storage by only allocating actual physical space when data is written, allowing administrators to over-allocate storage virtual space.

## Important Exam Points

  • Static vs. Dynamic IP: Watch out for true/false questions stating a Domain Controller can use a dynamic IP. This is False; it requires a static IP.
  • DNS Cache Checking: A local computer always checks its local DNS Cache and the local Hosts file before sending recursive queries out to a network DNS server.
  • Full Control vs. Modify vs. Write:
    • Full Control: Can modify, write, delete, and change security permissions.
    • Modify: Can read, write, and delete files.
    • Write: Can add or change files, but cannot delete.
  • Active Directory Database Paths:
    • Database path: C:\Windows\NTDS
    • Log path: C:\Windows\NTDS
    • SYSVOL path: C:\Windows\SYSVOL
  • Time Synchronization: Domain Controllers rely heavily on tight time synchronization (typically within 5 minutes) to maintain security protocols and Kerberos validation. Clocks must synchronize with a standard time source.
  • Windows Server 2019 GUI Management: The newly introduced web-based graphical management dashboard for Windows Server 2019 is the Windows Admin Center (WAC).

## Commonly Tested Topics from the Question Bank

  • File Server vs. Database Server: Understand that a database server stores large amounts of structured data and handles client queries, whereas a file server stores and shares unstructured user files.
  • Root Domain: The root domain is strictly defined as the very first domain established inside an Active Directory forest.
  • SYSVOL Folder Contents: SYSVOL stores Group Policy Objects (GPOs), system templates, and network scripts to keep active directory-wide behaviors consistent.
  • Active Directory Database Name: The logical database that holds AD object information (users, groups, machines) is the Directory Information Base (DIB).
  • Replication Definition: Replication duplicates directory database changes across multiple DCs to maintain data consistency and prevent a single point of failure.
  • OUs (Organizational Units): Designed to group directory objects to simplify administrative delegation and link group policies.
  • Basic vs. Dynamic Disks: Basic disks use standard partition tables, while Dynamic disks utilize dynamic volumes spanning multiple physical hard drives.
  • Spanned Volume Operation: A spanned volume writes data sequentially, filling up physical disk one completely before writing any data to physical disk two.
  • LIFDGE vs. CSVDE: While both perform batch imports of Active Directory user accounts, csvde.exe can only add new objects, whereas ldifde.exe can add, modify, and delete objects. (Note: Course syllabus flags this as not required for the exam but it is highly helpful background).

lessons.title: Introduction to Linux-System Installation Process and different Distros
lessons.content:
1. Definitions and Terminology

  • Linux: An open-source operating system based on UNIX.
  • Linux Kernel: The core of the Linux operating system. It acts as the central component that manages hardware resources and coordinates all software and hardware interactions.
  • Linux Distribution (Distro): A specific version of Linux (such as Ubuntu, Debian, or Fedora) that includes the Linux kernel, system tools, package managers, desktop environments, and pre-installed software.
  • Open Source: Software whose source code is freely available for anyone to inspect, modify, and distribute.
  • Package Manager: A built-in system utility (such as APT or YUM) that automates the installation, update, configuration, and removal of software packages.
  • Bootloader: A startup program responsible for loading the operating system into memory when the computer powers on.
  • Virtualization: The technology of running multiple isolated operating system environments simultaneously on a single physical machine.

2. Core Concepts and Analogies

  • The Kernel Conductor Analogy: The Linux kernel is compared to an orchestra conductor or a city traffic controller. It coordinates the activities of different computer components, making hardware like the CPU and memory available to running applications.
  • Kernel Size: While the kernel is the core of the OS, it is not the largest component of the operating system.
  • Desktop Environment (DE): The graphical interface of a distro. Its primary function is managing windows, menus, and visual interactions.
  • Linux in IoT (Internet of Things): Linux is highly favored in IoT because it can be customized and made extremely small to fit resource-constrained smart devices.
  • Historical Context: The Linux kernel was created by Linus Torvalds in 1994, written in the C programming language, and heavily influenced by Richard Stallman's GNU project and the educational MINIX operating system. Android is also a Linux-based operating system designed for smartphones.

3. Ubuntu Installation Process and Requirements

  • Primary System Verification: The installation process must always begin by checking the minimum system requirements.
  • Ubuntu System Requirements:
    • 25 GB of hard-drive space is required.
    • Note: 1 GB RAM, internet access, and a DVD drive are not mandatory requirements for basic installation.
  • Distro Classification: Debian, Red Hat, SUSE, Ubuntu, Mint, and Android are major distributions (distros), not kernel families.

lessons.title: Linux File tree system layout and Files systems
lessons.content:
1. File System Hierarchy and Philosophy

  • Structured Analogy: The Linux file system is organized in a hierarchical format starting from a single entry point. It is compared to a well-arranged library or a hierarchical filing cabinet.
  • "Everything is a File": In Linux, almost everything you interact with is treated as a file, including regular documents, folders (directories), and physical hardware components like printers.
    • Exception: A running process is not considered a file.
  • Inodes: A crucial data structure used by Linux to keep track of file details, metadata, and storage locations on the disk.

2. Directory Structures and Navigation Symbols

  • Root Directory (/): The top-level directory of the entire Linux file system.
  • User's Home Directory (~): Represented by the tilde symbol. Each regular user has a unique home directory under /home (e.g., /home/we is equivalent to ~).
  • Parent Directory (..): Used to refer to the directory immediately above the current working directory.

3. Navigation Paths

  • Absolute Path: A complete, exact path that starts from the root directory (/) and traces down to the target file. Example: /home/user/Documents.
  • Relative Path: A path that starts from the current working directory rather than the root directory.

4. Basic File and Directory Commands

  • pwd (Print Working Directory): Displays the full absolute path of the current folder you are in.
  • cd (Change Directory): Navigates between folders.
    • cd (without arguments): Automatically returns the user to their home directory (not /root).
    • cd ~: Moves directly to the user's home directory.
    • cd ..: Navigates up to the parent directory.
    • Troubleshooting: If a user attempts to navigate to a folder that does not exist, the terminal returns the error: "No such file or directory".
  • ls (List): Displays the contents of the current directory.
    • ls -a: Displays all files, including hidden files (hidden files in Linux are designated with a leading dot, e.g., .hidden_file).
    • ls -l: Displays file contents in long listing format, showing detailed metadata.

5. File Metadata Fields (ls -l output)

When executing ls -l, seven metadata fields are displayed from left to right:

  1. File Type & Permissions: Ten characters indicating the type of file (e.g., - for regular file, d for directory, l for symlink) followed by owner, group, and world read/write/execute permissions.
  2. Hard Link Count: The number of hard links/shortcuts pointing directly to the file data.
  3. User Owner: The specific user account that owns the file.
  4. Group Owner: The user group associated with the file.
  5. File Size: Typically displayed in bytes by default, but human-readable flags can display it in kilobytes or gigabytes.
  6. Modification Timestamp: The date and time the file was last modified.
  7. File Name: The actual name of the file or directory.

6. Symbolic Links vs. Hard Links

  • Symbolic Link (Soft Link): Works like a Windows shortcut; it is a pointer to the path of another file or directory.
    • Syntax: ln -s file1 link1.
    • Features: Can point to files or directories, can cross different file systems or partitions, and becomes broken (invalid) if the original source file is deleted.
  • Hard Link: Creates a direct duplicate reference to the same raw storage data on the disk.
    • Limitations: Cannot point to directories and cannot cross separate file systems. If the original file is deleted, the hard link still safely accesses the data.

lessons.title: Partitioning and formatting Disks
lessons.content:
1. Partitioning Schemes

  • MBR (Master Boot Record):
    • Limited to a maximum of 4 primary partitions.
    • Supports a maximum disk capacity of only 2 Terabytes (TB).
    • Consists of 3 parts.
  • GPT (GUID Partition Table):
    • A modern, highly flexible partitioning scheme.
    • Supports up to 128 primary partitions.
    • Features backup headers at the end of the disk for built-in data redundancy and safety.

2. Filesystems

  • EXT4: The default file system in modern Linux Ubuntu. It divides the partition into block groups to organize data efficiently and is highly recommended for general storage.
  • Other Filesystems: Linux supports other advanced file systems like ZFS, Btrfs, and XFS.
  • LVM (Logical Volume Manager): Provides dynamic, flexible logical disk management, allowing volume sizes to be resized easily.

3. Device Naming Conventions

  • Linux identifies hard drives using the device path scheme /dev/sd[letter].
  • sd stands for a SCSI or SATA device (not an older IDE device).
  • Example /dev/sdb1 Breakdown:
    • sd: SCSI or SATA disk.
    • b: The second physical hard disk detected by the system.
    • 1: The first partition on that second hard disk.
  • Note: A new device file like /dev/sdb1 is not accessible to users until it is formatted and mounted.

4. Disk Storage Commands

  • lsblk: Lists all block storage devices and active partitions in a tree layout.
    • lsblk -o NAME,UUID: Displays storage device names and their unique UUID (Universally Unique Identifier).
  • sudo fdisk -l: Lists all connected disks, partition tables, and sizing. Must be run with sudo/root privileges.
  • sudo fdisk /dev/sdb: Launches the interactive command-line partitioning menu for the second hard disk.
    • w: Saves the partition table changes to the disk and exits fdisk.
    • o: Creates a new empty MBR partition table.
  • mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1: Formats partition /dev/sdb1 with the EXT4 filesystem. Important: A partition must be formatted with a filesystem before it can store files.
  • df (Disk Free):
    • df -h: Displays free and used disk space in human-readable format (using GB, MB).
    • df -i / df -i -h: Displays inode usage statistics instead of block space.

5. Disk Mounting Concepts

  • Mounting: The process of attaching a formatted disk partition to a specific directory (the mount point) in the directory tree so its files can be accessed.
  • Administrative Prerequisite: Mounting can only be performed by the Root user. Standard users lack permissions.
  • Temporary vs. Persistent Mounting:
    • Executing sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/folder is a temporary mount. If the system restarts, this mount disappears; it remains only as a virtual memory link.
    • To make mounting permanent (available after restarts), you must configure it in the /etc/fstab file.

6. Persistent Mounting Configuration (/etc/fstab)

The file system configuration table /etc/fstab automates mounting at boot. It must be configured using UUIDs because they are guaranteed to be globally unique and persistent across hardware changes.

The table consists of 6 columns which MUST be separated by TABS (not spaces):

ColumnParameterDescription
1File SystemName or UUID of the device (e.g., UUID=xxxx... or /dev/sdb1).
2Mount PointDirectory path where the file system is attached (e.g., /home/we/Desktop/weschool).
3TypeThe filesystem format (e.g., ext4).
4OptionsMount options separated by commas (e.g., rw for read/write, exec to allow file execution, auto for boot mounting, nouser restricting mount to root).
5dumpLegacy backup setting (1 = backup, 0 = no backup). This utility is outdated and generally set to 0.
6passThe fsck file system check order at boot (0 = no check, 1 = root file system, 2 = all other partitions).

Note: The table's 6 columns must be separated by TABS, not spaces.

  • mount -a: Instantly mounts all storage devices listed in /etc/fstab.
  • systemctl daemon-reload: Reloads the systemd manager configuration. You must run this command after editing system mounting files to recognize the changes.

lessons.title: User and Group account management
lessons.content:
1. Types of Users

Linux identifies three main user types:

  1. Root User: The superuser with full system privileges (UID is always 0).
  2. Regular Users: Accounts created for people (UIDs start at 1000 and increment).
  3. System Accounts: Non-human system accounts (such as gdm or nm-openvpn) used to run specific software services.

2. User/Group Database Files

  • /etc/passwd: Stores basic user account details (username, UID, primary GID, home directory path, default shell).
  • /etc/shadow: Stores highly secure hashed user passwords and password aging settings. Only the root user has permission to read it.
  • /etc/group: Contains group names, group passwords, GIDs, and member lists.

3. User Administration Commands

  • useradd: The low-level utility to create user accounts. It is non-interactive.
    • Usage Example: sudo useradd -d /home/student -m student.
      • -d: Specifies the path to the home folder.
      • -m: Automatically creates the home folder if it doesn't exist.
    • UID Assignment Detail: When a user is added, they take the next available UID. For instance, if the latest user is student_we with UID 1003, the next user created (we-alex) will default to UID 1004.
  • adduser: A higher-level, highly interactive script that automatically creates the home directory, prompts for a password, and copies default startup files from /etc/skel. Not all distributions include it.
  • passwd: Sets or changes user passwords. Example: sudo passwd student.
  • userdel -r: Safely deletes a user account and removes their home folder and all personal files in one step.

4. Privilege Escalation and Switching Users

  • su (Switch User): Used to swap the current terminal session to another user account. Example: su student_we.
  • sudo (Super User Do): Allows standard users to run administrative commands with full root privileges.

5. Group Administration Commands

  • Primary Group: When a new user is created, Linux automatically creates a group with the exact same name as their Primary Group.
  • groupadd: Creates a new group. Example: groupadd students.
  • usermod -aG: Appends (-a) a user to a secondary group (-G). Example: sudo usermod -aG students student_we.
  • gpasswd: Can be used to manage groups, including removing a user from a group.

6. File & Directory Creation Commands

  • mkdir -p: Recursively creates nested directories and directory trees. Example: mkdir -p school/IT/unit13.
  • rmdir: Deletes a directory only when it is completely empty.
  • rm -r (or rm -R): Deletes a directory tree and all files inside it recursively.
  • cp: Copies files from source to destination.
  • mv: Moves or renames files. Note: When moving, the original copy is relocated to the destination.
  • touch: Creates empty files or updates timestamps.
    • touch we1 creates one file named we1.
    • touch we 1 (with a space) creates two separate files named we and 1.

7. File Permissions and Numeric vs. Symbolic Modes

  • chown: Changes user and group ownership of files and directories. Example: sudo chown student_we results.txt.
  • chmod: Modifies access permissions.
  • Numeric Mode: Permissions are calculated as octal sums: Read (r) = 4, Write (w) = 2, Execute (x) = 1.
    • Permissions blocks: User/Owner, Group, Others.
    • Example chmod 755: Owner gets rwx (7), Group gets r-x (5), Others get r-x (5).
  • Symbolic Mode: Uses letters (u=owner, g=group, o=others, a=all) and math operators.
    • Example chmod u+x file.txt: Adds execute permission only for the file owner.
    • Exam Warning: sudo chmod a=rwx file1 grants full read, write, and execute permissions to all users (equivalent to octal 777, NOT 747 or 552).

lessons.title: Networking Connection on Linux
lessons.content:
1. Setting Hostname

  • Hostname: A unique identifier assigned to a computer to identify it on a network.
  • Database File: The system hostname is persistently saved in /etc/hostname.
  • hostnamectl: Used to view or modify the system hostname.
    • Usage: sudo hostnamectl set-hostname "new_name".
  • Troubleshooting Hostname Resolution: If changing the hostname causes system errors (like "unable to resolve host"), you must manually edit /etc/hosts to bind the new hostname to the local loopback addresses (127.0.0.1).

2. Network Interfaces & IP Configuration

  • Domain Name System (DNS): Resolves human-readable domain names into computer-routable IP addresses.
  • iproute2 Suite: Modern networking suite that has officially replaced the deprecated net-tools utility suite.
  • ip addr show (or ip add show): Displays all active physical and virtual network interfaces along with their assigned IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
  • ifconfig: An obsolete command from the deprecated net-tools suite.
  • Interface UP: sudo ip link set ens33 up.
  • Interface DOWN: sudo ip link set ens33 down.

3. Monitoring and Managing Linux Processes

  • Process: A running instance of a system program or command.
  • PID: A unique Process ID assigned by the system to monitor and track each active process.
  • ps (Process Status): Displays a static snapshot of active terminal processes.
    • ps aux: Displays extensive, detailed metadata for every running process on the system.
    • ps -u username: Filters and shows processes running for a specific user.
  • top: A dynamic, real-time interactive process viewer.
    • Press q to quit the top program safely.
    • Press k inside top to kill a process by entering its PID.
  • htop: A modern, interactive, and highly user-friendly dynamic process monitoring tool.
  • kill [PID]: Sends a standard termination signal to gracefully stop a running process.
  • kill -9 [PID]: Sends a SIGKILL signal to forcefully terminate an unresponsive or frozen process.

Study Synthesis

1. Key Points to Remember

  • Almost everything in Linux is structured as a file, except running processes.
  • Linux kernel development was founded by Linus Torvalds, written in C, and coordinated hardware interaction like a conductor.
  • The primary partition limit for MBR tables is exactly 4, with a capacity limit of 2 TB.
  • SATA and SCSI hard drives are designated /dev/sd[letter]. /dev/sdb1 represents partition 1 on the second disk.
  • Regular user accounts in Ubuntu begin taking UIDs starting from 1000.
  • The /etc/shadow file contains hashed passwords and is readable only by the root user.
  • Network configuration has migrated from the deprecated net-tools suite (ifconfig) to the modern iproute2 suite (ip addr show).

2. Important Exam Points

  • MBR Disk Size & Partition Limits: You cannot create more than 4 primary partitions under MBR, and it does not support disks larger than 2 TB.
  • MBR DOS Command flag: In fdisk, the key to initialize an MBR DOS partition table is o.
  • Temporary vs. Permanent Mounts: Direct mount commands are lost upon reboot. Permanent mounts require modifying /etc/fstab.
  • Tab Separators: Spacing errors (using spaces instead of tabs) in /etc/fstab columns will crash mounting procedures.
  • Symlink Constraints: Symbolic links can cross different file systems and point to folders. Hard links are confined to a single file system and cannot point to folders.
  • File Ownership Count: Unlike Windows, a Linux file can be owned by exactly one user and one group at a time.
  • Hashed Passwords Storage: If asked where encrypted passwords are saved, the answer is /etc/shadow. Basic account settings are in /etc/passwd.

3. Commonly Tested Topics from the Question Bank

  • Command Differences (useradd vs. adduser): useradd is low-level and non-interactive, while adduser is interactive.
  • Homedir Shortcut: Navigating to ~ or executing cd without options returns you directly to /home/username.
  • Recursive Deletion (rm -r vs. rmdir): Empty folders are deleted with rmdir. Folders containing files must be deleted using rm -r.
  • File Size Storage Scale: While byte-scale representation is default, metadata outputs also scale dynamically to Kilobytes and Gigabytes.
  • Permission Translations: Knowing the exact numeric translation (e.g., chmod 755 or understanding that a=rwx translates to 777).
  • Interface State Up/Down: The exact ip link set [interface] up/down syntax.
  • Dynamic Monitoring Exit: The q key is used to exit the interactive top utility.

lessons.title: VLAN Trunking Protocol
lessons.content:
Definitions and Terminology

  • VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP): A Cisco proprietary protocol used to distribute and synchronize identifying information about VLANs configured throughout a switched network.
  • VTP Domain: A group of switches sharing the same VLAN details4. VTP configuration requires domain names to be identical on switches for VTP messages to synchronize56.
  • Configuration Revision Number: A 32-bit number that tracks database changes7. It starts at zero and increases by 1 every time a VLAN is added, modified, or deleted78. A switch uses this number to determine if its local database is outdated7.
  • Primary Server: Introduced in VTP Version 3, this switch has the final authority over making database changes and propagates updates to other switches.

Important Concepts and VTP Modes

VTP allows network administrators to configure VLANs on a single server switch, which automatically propagates those updates to all other switches in the domain3. VTP messages only propagate across trunk links.

Switches can be configured in one of four distinct VTP operating modes11:

  1. Server Mode (Default): The switch can create, change, and delete VLAN configurations. It saves VLAN settings in NVRAM, sends out VTP updates, and applies incoming updates14.
  2. Client Mode: The switch receives, applies, and forwards VTP updates but cannot create, modify, or delete VLANs locally. Settings are not saved in NVRAM and are lost upon reboot.
  3. Transparent Mode: The switch handles its VLANs only locally112. It can create and delete its own local VLANs5, but these do not propagate to other switches. It completely ignores incoming VTP updates but forwards (passes along) VTP updates to downstream switches.
  4. Off Mode: The switch behaves purely locally for VLAN management12 and completely ignores, drops, and does not forward VTP advertisements810.

VTP Advertisements

VTP messages are sent out using a multicast address813.

  • VTP advertisements occur every 300 seconds (5 minutes), or immediately after any VLAN database change occurs16.
  • Summary Advertisements: Include the VTP version, domain name, configuration revision number, and a timestamp713.
  • Subset Advertisements: Sent out immediately following a VLAN change, containing the actual VLAN parameters and configuration details.

Troubleshooting and VTP Design Constraints

  • Verification Command: The primary command to verify VTP configuration is show vtp status. This displays active VTP version, domain name, VTP mode, maximum supported local VLANs, configuration revision number, and MD5 digest14.
  • The VTP Off-Mode Fatal Mistake: It is a critical design error to place a client-mode switch downstream from an off-mode switch. Because the off-mode switch ignores and does not forward VTP messages810, the client switch will be completely cut off from receiving VTP database updates.
  • VTPv3 Advantages: Supports a larger VLAN range (up to 4094, including extended range)19, allows better control via a single Primary Server1019, and prevents accidental configuration overwrites.

lessons.title: Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol
lessons.content:
Definitions and Spanning Tree Variations

  • Spanning Tree Protocol (STP - 802.1D): Standardized as IEEE 802.1D20. It is designed to prevent Layer 2 bridging loops in redundant network topologies by blocking redundant ports. It is slow to converge, typically requiring 50 seconds to transition a port to active state2023.
  • Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP - 802.1w): Standardized as IEEE 802.1w24. It provides much faster convergence (typically within 10 seconds or less of a topology change)20. RSTP introduces the Alternate port (acting as a backup path to the root bridge) and the Backup port. It combines blocking, listening, and disabled states into a single discarding state.
  • Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus (PVST+): A Cisco proprietary implementation of STP that runs a separate spanning tree instance for every configured VLAN. This optimizes path selection for individual VLANs2831, but introduces high CPU and memory overhead on switches2732.
  • Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol (MSTP - 802.1s): Standardized as IEEE 802.1s24. It optimizes switch resources by allowing multiple VLANs to share the same spanning tree instance, reducing resource consumption while preserving traffic load-balancing.

Bridge ID (BID) and MAC Address Reduction

With the introduction of the IEEE 802.1Q standard, the original Bridge ID (BID) format (which used a 2-byte priority and 6-byte MAC address) was updated to support a System ID Extension34.

The split priority system consists of:

  1. Priority (4 bits): Modifiable in increments of 4096 (e.g., 0, 4096, 8192, up to 61440)32. Default is 327686.
  2. System ID Extension (12 bits): Typically maps directly to the VLAN ID and cannot be changed.
  3. System ID (6 bytes): The physical MAC address of the switch.

Calculating the Total Bridge Priority

Total Priority = Configured Bridge Priority + VLAN ID (System ID Extension)

  • Example: If a switch is running in PVST+ mode for VLAN 30 and has its base priority configured as 24576, the total priority value advertised in its BPDUs is 24576 + 30 = 2460634.
  • Root Bridge Election: The switch with the lowest Bridge ID (BID) is elected as the Root Bridge3637. If priorities are identical, the switch with the lowest MAC address wins34.

lessons.title: PortFast and BPDU Guard
lessons.content:
Definitions and Spanning Tree Security Features

  • PortFast: An STP optimization feature configured on ports connected strictly to end-user hosts (e.g., PCs, printers, servers).
  • BPDU Guard: A Layer 2 security feature designed to shut down PortFast-enabled ports if they detect incoming Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs).

PortFast Mechanics and DHCP Assistance

  • Normally, an STP-enabled switch port takes about 50 seconds to transition to active forwarding state as it cycles through listening and learning phases to detect loops.
  • Enabling PortFast allows the port to bypass listening and learning phases, immediately transitioning to the forwarding state upon physical connection.
  • DHCP Performance: Bypassing the 50-second delay prevents DHCP client timeouts, allowing hosts to receive IP address configurations instantly upon link-up.
  • Critical Restriction: PortFast must never be enabled on switch-to-switch links. Doing so bypasses STP checks, creating a high risk of loop formation if a loop physically exists.

BPDU Guard Mechanics

  • Because PortFast bypasses loop checks, connecting an unauthorized switch or looping a PortFast-enabled port can cause catastrophic network failure.
  • BPDU Guard prevents this vulnerability40. If any BPDU is received on a PortFast port, BPDU Guard immediately disables the interface and places it in an err-disabled (error-disabled) state.
  • Trunk Port Warning: Activating BPDU Guard on a trunk port is highly disruptive, as it will disable the trunk port and completely halt all communications crossing it40.

Configuration Commands

  • Enable PortFast Globally: Enables PortFast on all access ports:

spanning-tree portfast default

  • Enable BPDU Guard Globally: Activates BPDU Guard on all PortFast-enabled ports:

spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default

  • Enable BPDU Guard on a Specific Interface:

spanning-tree bpduguard enable

lessons.title: EtherChannel Bundle and load balance
lessons.content:
Definitions and Operational Concepts

  • EtherChannel: A link aggregation technology that groups multiple physical Ethernet interfaces into a single logical, high-speed connection called a port-channel.
  • Port-Channel: The logical interface created by combining physical links. A switch can bundle up to 16 physical links, combining up to 8 active links in a single port-channel53.
  • EtherChannel Guard (Misconfiguration Guard): A protocol check that automatically detects parameter mismatches on either side of the channel, disabling mismatched links to preserve Layer 2 loop-free stability.

Interaction with Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)

  • Without EtherChannel, connecting redundant links between switches causes Spanning Tree to block all but one link to prevent Layer 2 loops5154.
  • STP treats an EtherChannel group as a single logical link58. As a result, STP does not block the redundant physical links in the bundle, allowing all active interfaces to forward traffic simultaneously, increasing aggregate bandwidth and providing fast redundancy.

Dynamic Negotiation Protocols and Modes

  1. Port Aggregation Protocol (PAgP): Cisco Proprietary protocol.
    • Desirable Mode: Actively initiates negotiation.
    • Auto Mode: Passively responds to negotiation (does not initiate).
  2. Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP): Open IEEE standard5860.
    • Active Mode: Actively initiates negotiation.
    • Passive Mode: Passively responds to negotiation.
  3. On Mode: Forces the interfaces to channel immediately without exchanging dynamic negotiation packets24. Both sides must be set to "On"24.

Layer 2 vs. Layer 3 EtherChannel

  • Layer 2 EtherChannel: Operates as standard switchports (access or trunk links)61.
  • Layer 3 EtherChannel: Operates as a routed interface61. Configuring Layer 3 EtherChannel requires running the no switchport command on the physical interfaces before bundling them into the port-channel, allowing an IP address to be configured directly on the port-channel interface.

Configuration Requirements

All physical ports placed inside an EtherChannel must have matching:

  • Speed and Duplex settings5763.
  • Switchport mode (trunk or access)59.
  • Allowed VLAN list and Native VLAN59.

Troubleshooting and Monitoring

  • Verification Command: show etherchannel summary.
  • Port Status Meanings:
    • "RU" Flags: Indicates the logical port-channel is in Layer 3 (Routing) and is active/in-use ("U")5658.
    • "P" Flag: The physical port is successfully bundled in the port-channel59.
    • "w" Flag (Waiting): The physical port is waiting for negotiation to complete59.
    • "s" Flag (Suspended): The port is disabled due to a negotiation or configuration mismatch59.
  • Suspended Troubleshooting Case: If port Eth0/1 on Switch 1 displays waiting ("w") and Eth0/1 on Switch 2 displays suspended ("s"), troubleshooting must start on Switch 259. A suspended status indicates a severe mismatch (such as mismatched speed, duplex, trunking, or negotiation dynamic protocols)59.

lessons.title: Power over Ethernet
lessons.content:
Definitions and Key Components

  • Power over Ethernet (PoE): A technology that delivers both DC power and data through a single Ethernet UTP cable.
  • Power Sourcing Equipment (PSE): The device (typically a network switch) that injects and supplies DC power over the Ethernet cable.
  • Powered Device (PD): The end device that accepts power from the Ethernet cable instead of a local AC outlet3069 (e.g., IP cameras, IP phones, and wireless access points)6167.

Benefits of PoE

  • Reduces installation complexity and cost by using a single cable for both data and power.
  • Enables deployment of network devices in remote locations where electrical outlets are difficult or costly to install.
  • Provides centralized power management and backup capability from the wiring closet.

PoE Standards and Capacities (Maximum Power at PSE)

The maximum power delivered at the PSE varies by standard:

PoE StandardMaximum Power at PSEWire Pairs UsedKey Supported Devices
Cisco Inline Power7 Watts2 PairsEarly IP Phones
IEEE 802.3af (PoE)15.4 Watts2 PairsStandard IP Phones, basic IP cameras
IEEE 802.3at (PoE+)30 Watts2 PairsPTZ cameras, Dual-band Access Points
IEEE 802.3bt (UPoE)60 Watts4 PairsVideo IP phones, higher-power APs
IEEE 802.3bt (UPoE+)100 Watts4 PairsComputer screens, LED lighting, thin clients

Monitoring and Verification Commands

  • Verify Power Delivery: show power inline. This displays the active PoE status on switch ports, the exact power allocated, and the current power consumption utilized by connected PDs.

Detection and Power Negotiation Process

  • Before applying high-voltage DC power, the PSE runs an auto-negotiation signature detection process to determine if a connected device is a valid PD requiring power.
  • If the connected hardware does not require power, no power is sent, protecting standard devices from damage6871.
  • If a valid PD is detected, the PSE determines its exact power class and reduces its power output to safely match the device's specific consumption needs.

1. Key Points to Remember

  • VTP advertisements are multicast, sent every 300 seconds, and carry the configuration revision number.
  • VTP transparent mode switches do not apply VTP changes but do forward VTP advertisements to downstream switches.
  • The default VTP operating mode on Cisco Catalyst switches is Server Mode2.
  • The system ID extension in the Spanning Tree Bridge ID uses 12 bits and represents the VLAN ID634.
  • Adjusting bridge priority values must be done in increments of 4096.
  • RSTP (IEEE 802.1w) converges in under 10 seconds20 and introduces the discarding port state2530 alongside Alternate and Backup port roles.
  • PortFast immediately transitions access ports to the forwarding state, skipping listening and learning.
  • BPDU Guard protects PortFast ports by shutting them down and placing them in an err-disabled state upon detecting any BPDU.
  • STP treats an EtherChannel group as a single logical link58, allowing redundant physical links to remain unblocked5455.
  • EtherChannel dynamic protocols are PAgP (Cisco proprietary) and LACP (IEEE standard)5860.
  • no switchport is the mandatory first command on a physical port when building a routed Layer 3 EtherChannel.
  • PoE delivers DC power and data safely through a single Ethernet UTP cable.
  • A PoE switch acts as the PSE (Power Sourcing Equipment), whereas an IP phone acts as a PD (Powered Device)3069.

2. Important Exam Points

  • VTP Off-Mode Behavior: A switch in VTP Off mode will ignore and will not forward VTP advertisements810. If a client switch is placed after an Off-mode switch, it will never receive VLAN configuration propagation.
  • VTP Client Mode Restrictions: Switchports on VTP Client-mode switches cannot configure or alter VLAN databases locally.
  • Spanning Tree Bridge ID Calculation: Be prepared to calculate the total bridge priority. For priority class 32768 on VLAN 10, the advertised priority in the BID is 32768 + 10 = 3277834.
  • RSTP Convergence: RSTP usually converges within 10 seconds of a topology change20 compared to STP's 50 seconds2023.
  • PortFast Deployment Risk: PortFast should only be deployed on ports connected to workstations, printers, or servers. Applying PortFast to switch-to-switch links can cause catastrophic Layer 2 loops.
  • EtherChannel Status Troubleshooting: If an interface displays an "s" (suspended) flag inside show etherchannel summary, start troubleshooting at the suspended switch59. Common causes are speed, duplex, native VLAN mismatches, or PAgP/LACP negotiation failure59.
  • PoE Standards Capacity Matrix: Ensure you memorize the maximum power outputs at the PSE:
    • Cisco Inline Power: 7W
    • 802.3af (PoE): 15.4W
    • 802.3at (PoE+): 30W
    • 802.3bt (UPoE): 60W
    • 802.3bt (UPoE+): 100W

3. Commonly Tested Topics from the Question Bank

  • VTP Creator: Created by Cisco1.
  • VTP Stand For: VLAN Trunking Protocol1.
  • Summary Advertisement Elements: Revision number and timestamp13.
  • VTP default mode: Server2.
  • Original Spanning Tree Standard: IEEE 802.1D20.
  • IEEE Standard for RSTP: IEEE 802.1w24.
  • EtherChannel dynamic protocols: PAgP (Cisco proprietary) and LACP (IEEE standard)5860.
  • EtherChannel Misconfig Guard Global Command: switchport etherchannel guard misconfig5763.
  • Layer 3 conversion command: no switchport.
  • PoE PSE device example: Switch.
  • PoE Class verification: show power inline.
  • PoE 802.3at Power Capacity: 30 Watts3072.
  • UPoE+ Power Capacity: 100 Watts6972

lessons.title: Soft and Hard planning for your LAN network
lessons.content:
Network infrastructure serves as the foundational architecture enabling schools and organizations to share information, communicate, and conduct online classes. Not all networks are identical; organizations must customize their setup based on their budget, usability, reliability, security, and scalability requirements. Designing a network always requires two critical phases: Soft Planning and Hard Planning.

I. Soft Planning (The Phase of Ideas)

Soft planning represents the early conceptualization and logical layout of the network before any equipment is purchased or installed.

  1. Needs Assessment:
    • Purpose determination: Defining exactly what the network will be used for (e.g., file sharing, communication, or online learning).
    • User capacity planning: Assessing how many users will access the network and their demand levels to ensure it does not slow down under heavy traffic.
  2. Design Considerations:
    • Logical Layout: Plan showing how devices (computers, printers, etc.) connect and how data moves/flows through the network.
    • IP Addressing: Assigning a unique numeric address to every device so data is routed to the correct destination, similar to physical mail.
    • Network Segmentation: Splitting a large network into smaller, manageable parts (like dividing students into classes) to simplify network administration and apply specific rules.
  3. Security Planning:
    • Firewall: Acts as a virtual security guard, inspecting traffic to allow authorized packets and block harmful traffic.
    • Antivirus Software: Acts like a doctor, searching for, identifying, and eliminating harmful viruses or programs.
    • Updates and User Education: Regularly updating software and educating users to recognize scams and protect their personal information. Regular updates and education are mandatory security components.
  4. Budgeting:
    • Planning immediate setup costs (software, computers, cables, routers).
    • Planning long-term operational costs (replacement parts, software upgrades, technical support). Exam Note: Budgeting must never only consider initial setup costs.

II. Hard Planning (The Phase of Physical Decisions)

Hard planning focuses on selecting hardware, organizing the physical layout, and scheduling installations.

  1. Physical Layout: Deciding where to place servers and other network equipment, and determining the routing paths and types of cables. Exam Note: Server physical layouts are strictly decided in hard planning, not soft planning.
  2. Hardware Selection: Choosing switches, routers, and servers based on performance, speed, and power requirements. Exam Note: Hardware selection must account for future scalability and expansion.
  3. Implementation Plan: Establishing a step-by-step schedule to deploy the network, and evaluating how the installation process might disrupt normal daily operations.

lessons.title: Physical Media - Cable Properties
lessons.content:
Physical cables form the backbone of a wired local area network (LAN). Choosing the correct physical media requires assessing data speed, maximum distances, and interference risks.

I. Cable Performance Factors

  • Speed: Core connections (the main/central part of a network backbone where major data aggregates) require ultra-high speeds up to 10 Gbps (10 billion bits per second). Access connections (where end-user devices connect) can operate at standard speeds.
  • Distance: Office copper cables have strict length boundaries. A standard Ethernet office cable can run up to 100 meters without signal loss or degradation.
  • Interference & Security: Electrical noise from surrounding electronics degrades copper signals. Fiber optic cables send data using light, making them immune to electrical interference (EMI/RFI) and highly secure against signal eavesdropping/spying.

II. Cable Types and Applications

  1. Shielded Twisted Pair (STP):
    • Contains internal twisted wires with an extra protective shield to block electronic noise.
    • Highly suited for industrial settings, businesses, or high-noise environments (e.g., a gaming cafe with crowded electronic devices).
    • Typically more expensive than UTP.
  2. Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP):
    • Lacks an extra shield but is engineered with twisted wire pairs to reduce crosstalk.
    • More affordable and suitable for quiet, controlled, low-interference indoor environments (e.g., a standard school computer lab).
  3. Fiber Optic Cables:
    • Transmit data using light pulses through thin glass or plastic strands.
    • Deliver extreme speeds, robust security against spying, and carry signals across massive distances (up to 40 km).
    • Frequently deployed for uplinks (connections that link smaller switches to larger network backbones) and linking different buildings.

III. Twisted Pair Categories & Naming Standards

Twisting copper wires together actively cancels out electromagnetic interference to keep the signal strong.

Cable Base NameTechnical Standard NameMaximum DistanceMaximum SpeedCable Type
Category 6 (Cat6)1000BASE-T / 10GBASE-T100 m (1000BASE-T) / 55 m (10GBASE-T)1 Gbps (1000 Mbps) / 10 GbpsUTP / UTP
Category 6a (Cat6a / Cat6A)10GBASE-T100 m10 GbpsUTP
Category 7 (Cat7)10GBASE-T100 m10 GbpsSTP
Category 8 (Cat8)25GBASE-T / 40GBASE-T30 m25 Gbps / 40 GbpsSTP

Technical Terminology Breakdown:

  • The "10" in 10GBASE-T stands for a data speed of 10 Gbps.
  • The "1000" in 1000BASE-T indicates support for 1 Gbps (1000 Mbps).
  • Exam Note: The "T" in these standard names does NOT stand for "transmission".

IV. Fiber Optic Classifications

  • Single-Mode Fiber (SMF): Built to carry data over extremely long distances at massive bandwidths. It is used for broad internet backbones linking cities or countries.
  • Multi-Mode Fiber (MMF): Built to transport data across shorter distances, such as inside data centers or single office buildings.

V. Structured Cabling System & Installation

A structured cabling system is a planned, organized method of running cables inside a building. Design is dictated by building size, node requirement per room, and future expansion.

  • Node Allocation Rules: Standard classrooms require 2 to 3 network nodes (ports), while specialized computer labs need 20 to 30 nodes. Every single node must have its own dedicated cable.
  • Cable Routing: Cables route from rooms to a central point. Vertical runs between floors utilize dedicated utility paths called risers.
  • Labeling Protocol: Cables must be labeled during installation to enable seamless troubleshooting and upgrades. Labels are typically made of Tyvek, a highly durable, tear-resistant, and safe material that will not damage cables. These labels are distributed in rolls or flat sheets.
  • Cable Trays: Rigid trays must be used during installation to organize and hold cables neatly.

lessons.title: Installing wiring Distribution (MDF/IDF)
lessons.content:
This lesson traces how cables exit walls, consolidate in distribution rooms, and plug into physical networking hardware.

I. The Physical Path of the Signal

Network cables run behind walls, under raised floors, or above ceiling tiles (requiring ladders to access).

  1. The Faceplate: Mounted on the wall, containing an RJ45 wall socket.
  2. Horizontal Cable: Runs behind the wall from the faceplate to the distribution room.
  3. The Patch Panel: A passive, metal terminal board where all building cables terminate. It serves as a central hub to organize cables, protect switches from physical wear, and simplify upgrades.
  4. The Patch Cord: A short, flexible Ethernet cable that bridges the port on the patch panel to a port on the network switch.

II. Copper Wiring Standards

Twisted pair copper cables contain 8 colored wires that must be mapped to 8 pins at both ends using industry-standard configurations.

  • T568A Standard: Green wires map to pins 1 & 2; orange wires map to pins 3 & 6.
  • T568B Standard: Orange wires map to pins 1 & 2; green wires map to pins 3 & 6.
  • Exam Note: The only difference between T568A and T568B is the arrangement/placement of the green and orange wires.
  • Cable Configurations:
    • Straight-through cable: Wired identically at both ends (standard device-to-switch connection).
    • Crossover cable: Green and orange pairs are swapped at one end.
    • Exam Note: For combined voice and data transmission on a single cable, all eight (8) wires must be terminated and connected correctly.

III. Fiber Distribution and Media Conversion

  • Optical Distribution Frame (ODF): A highly specialized patch panel engineered specifically for fiber optic cables. It organizes fiber lines, protects fragile glass strands, and allows administrators to redirect lines or make repairs without shutting down the network.
  • Media Converter: A physical transceiver used to translate signals between incompatible media (e.g., transforming a single-mode or multi-mode fiber connection into copper Ethernet).

IV. Server Racks and Cabinets

  • Networking gear is housed in strong metal frames called racks.
  • Height is measured in standard Rack Units (U).
  • One Rack Unit (1U) equals exactly 1.75 inches in height.
  • Design Example: To support 40 classrooms, an administrator must select a patch panel with at least 48 ports, select an appropriately sized rack (U-height), and verify future expansion capabilities.

V. Critical Installation Tools

  • Punch-down Tool: Specifically designed to press copper wires securely into patch panels or wall jacks and trim excess wire. Warning: Screwdrivers or incorrect tools must never be used, as they ruin connectors.
  • Crimper: Tool utilized to attach RJ45 plastic modular plugs to raw copper cable ends.
  • Cable Tester / Fiber Cable Tester: Devices used to verify wire maps and diagnose signal breaks.

lessons.title: Contracts and Cables
lessons.content:
Building enterprise-grade network infrastructure requires establishing binding legal agreements before starting work (contracts) and recording precise technical details after deployment (documentation).

I. Infrastructure Contracts

A contract plans the project and protects both the customer and the provider from cost overruns or schedule delays.

  1. Scope of Work: Explains exactly what tasks, upgrades, or hardware installations will be executed.
  2. Timeline: Defines milestones, task durations, and final project delivery dates.
  3. Costs and Payments: Details the total pricing and schedule of payments.
  4. Quality Standards: Defines how well the final network must perform and its reliability thresholds.
  5. Responsibilities: Outlines who is responsible for purchasing gear, doing the labor, and validating final operations.

II. Network Documentation

Documentation is the operator's manual for the network. It is crucial for troubleshooting, future upgrades, and training new administrators.

  1. Network Diagram: A detailed map showing the physical and logical links between routers, switches, and other devices.
  2. Inventory List: A list recording every device's brand, model, physical location, and current software/firmware version.
  3. Configuration Files: Exact backup settings that control device behavior, security rules, and user permissions.

III. Ethernet Switch Configuration Commands

The student guide details real CLI commands used to configure a managed distribution switch (assigning VLANs, IP settings, DHCP pools, security, LLDP, and SNMP settings):

1. VLAN Initialization

# Create local Virtual Local Area Networks and assign numeric tags

create vlan Data-Mcit tag 200

create vlan WirelessMgnt tag 300

create vlan mgnt tag 100

2. VLAN Port Mapping (Trunk/Tagged Ports)

# Bind 802.1Q tagging to trunk ports connecting to other switches or core routers

configure vlan mgnt add ports 1,2,21,22,23,24,25,26,27,28 tagged

configure vlan WirelessMgnt add ports 1,2,21,22,23,24,25,26,27,28 tagged

configure vlan Data-Mcit add ports 1,2,21,22,23,24,25,26,27,28 tagged

3. Switch IP Interfaces

# Assign management and interface IP addresses to VLANs

configure vlan Data-Mcit ipaddress 10.0.8.2/21

configure vlan mgnt ipaddress 10.0.0.1/21

4. DHCP Server Pool Configuration

# Establish dynamic IP address distribution pool, default gateways, and DNS settings

configure vlan Data-Mcit dhcp-address-range 10.0.8.3 - 10.0.15.254

configure vlan Data-Mcit dhcp-options default-gateway 10.0.8.1

configure vlan Data-Mcit dhcp-options dns-server primary 8.8.8.8

configure vlan Data-Mcit dhcp-options dns-server secondary 8.8.4.4

enable dhcp ports 1,2,21,22,23,24,25,26,27,28 vlan Data-Mcit

5. Local Security & Web Access

# Secure the switch console/remote administration and enable HTTP web access

configure account admin password "Mcit@123"

configure account user password

enable web http

6. Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) Advertisements

# Enable LLDP globally and configure standard TLV advertisements for neighbor discovery

enable lldp ports all

configure lldp ports all advertise all-tlvs

configure lldp ports all advertise management-address

configure lldp ports all advertise port-description

Configure lldp port all advertise system-capabilities

configure lldp ports all advertise system-description

configure lldp ports all advertise system-name

configure lldp port all advertise vendor-specific med capabilities

7. SNMPv3 Network Management Configuration

# Set system identity and location details, and establish secure SNMPv3 user authentication

configure snmp sysName "Co-Dist"

configure snmp sysLocation "Mcit-Wadi"

configure snmp sysContact "SoulcoEG"

enable snmp access snmpv3

configure snmpv3 add user snmpuser authentication md5 snmpauthcred privacy des snmpprivcred

configure snmpv3 add mib-view internet subtree 1 type included

configure snmpv3 add group SNMPG user snmpuser sec-model usm

lessons.title: Access points Installation - Devices configuration
lessons.content:
Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs) allow modern computing devices to connect to internet resources without physical tethering.

I. Frequency Spectrum Analysis

Wireless communication propagates via two main frequency bands, each featuring distinct trade-offs:

  • 2.4 GHz Frequency Band:
    • Pros: Outstanding physical propagation, offering a longer range and the ability to penetrate solid walls or obstacles effectively.
    • Cons: Substantially slower maximum data speeds and highly congested/crowded. Many common appliances (e.g., microwaves, baby monitors, cordless phones) operate here, causing signal interference.
  • 5 GHz Frequency Band:
    • Pros: Delivers much faster speeds, higher bandwidth, and a clearer connection due to less device crowding.
    • Cons: Significantly shorter range and poor wall penetration. It struggles to pass through solid concrete barriers.

II. Wireless Identifiers

  • SSID (Service Set Identifier): The user-friendly, broadcasted name of the wireless network (e.g., "School-Guest"). Note: It is not a secret access code.
  • BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier): The unique, low-level MAC address of the specific Access Point radio broadcasting the SSID.

III. Wireless Access Point (AP) Deployment Modes

Access Points bridge wireless clients to the wired infrastructure. They operate in two primary deployment modes:

  1. Autonomous (Standalone) APs:
    • Operate completely independently without requiring a centralized controller.
    • All settings, security rules, and firmware updates must be manually applied to each device individually.
    • Suited for home networks or very small offices requiring only a few APs.
    • Switch Link Requirement: Standalone APs can map local wireless users to different VLANs; therefore, the physical switch port must be configured as a trunk link.
  2. Lightweight APs:
    • Cannot function independently; they act as passive devices that fetch all settings and rules from a central controller.
    • Managed centrally by a Wireless LAN Controller (WLC).
    • Perfect for large office spaces or schools. If a firmware patch is required, the WLC pushes it to hundreds of APs simultaneously with one command.
    • Switch Link Requirement: Because lightweight APs delegate VLAN tagging to the controller, the physical switch port must be configured as an access link.

IV. CAPWAP Protocol Operations

  • CAPWAP stands for Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points.
  • It creates a secure virtual tunnel between each lightweight AP and the WLC.
  • CAPWAP encapsulates (wraps) all user data and management commands into secure packets, allowing centralized traffic control across the routers and switches of the enterprise network.

Key Summaries & Exam Preparation

1. Key Points to Remember

  • Logical vs. Physical Layouts: The logical layout maps data flows, IP schemes, and VLAN segmentations. The physical layout maps cable routing, server rooms, and device locations.
  • Cabling Distances: Copper twisted pair Ethernet cables are limited to a maximum run of 100 meters. Category 8 copper is limited to 30 meters. Fiber optic can run up to 40 km.
  • Wiring Color Maps: T568A and T568B differ strictly in the placement of the green and orange wire pairs.
  • Voice/Data Convergence: A single cable carrying both telephone voice and network data must have all 8 internal wires terminated properly.
  • Rack Height Standard: Hardware height is measured in Rack Units (U), where 1U is exactly 1.75 inches tall.
  • WLAN Frequencies: 2.4 GHz trades off speed for better distance and wall penetration. 5 GHz trades off distance for speed and a clear, uncrowded signal.
  • AP Port Configurations: Autonomous APs require trunk switch ports. Lightweight APs require access switch ports.

2. Important Exam Points

  • Design Budget Limits: Budgeting must consider future repairs, licensing, and upgrades---never just the initial purchase prices.
  • Tool Discipline: Only use a specialized punch-down tool to wire patch panels and wall faceplates. Screwdrivers or knives will damage physical copper pins.
  • "T" does not mean Transmission: In standard Ethernet naming (like 1000BASE-T), the "T" does not stand for transmission.
  • VLAN tagged configuration: In the MCIT CLI configurations, trunks mapping multiple VLANs must have their port bindings explicitly set to tagged.
  • CAPWAP Role: CAPWAP handles data encapsulation and tunneling between lightweight APs and the WLC.

3. Commonly Tested Topics from the Question Bank

  • Security Definitions: Understanding that firewalls act as security guards and antivirus software acts like a doctor checking for harmful programs.
  • Switch Purchase Decisions: When purchasing a new switch, the most important features to evaluate are:
    • Ports speed
    • Access (Layer 2) vs. Managed (Layer 3) switch type
    • PoE (Power over Ethernet) support
    • Price
  • Key Infrastructure Tools: You must be able to list and identify:
    • Punch-down tool (for terminal blocks/patch panels)
    • Crimper (for RJ45 modular plug termination)
    • Cable Tester (for copper wire verification)
    • Fiber Cable Tester (for fiber optic troubleshooting)
  • SSID Myths: The SSID is merely the broadcasted name of the network, not a security password or encryption key
